tool.name: Rust
tool.tagline: Fast, memory-safe systems language with no garbage collector
tool.description: Rust is a compiled systems programming language that guarantees memory and thread safety at compile time through ownership and borrowing, without a garbage collector. It is used for command-line tools, web services, embedded firmware, WebAssembly, and performance-critical parts of browsers, operating systems and cloud infrastructure. Learning it teaches you to reason precisely about ownership, lifetimes and concurrency.

glossary.def: Rust's official helper tool. It creates projects, builds and runs them, runs their tests and downloads shared code packages.
The installer and updater for Rust. It installs the compiler and Cargo and keeps them up to date.
Rust's word for one unit of code the compiler builds: a program or a library. Shared crates are published on crates.io for anyone to use.
The default way Cargo builds a program: quick to compile and easy to inspect, but much slower to run.
A build made with `cargo build --release`: slower to compile, but fully speed-tuned. Use it whenever you measure performance.
A named set of small language rules (2015, 2018, 2021, 2024) that a project opts into in Cargo.toml. Code from different editions still works together.
Code between curly braces { }. In Rust a block also produces a value: the value of its last expression.
One of the alternative paths in an if/else or a match; only one of them runs.
The smallest unit of computer data: a single 0 or 1. Eight bits make a byte.
A note added to code for the compiler or other tools, such as a type annotation saying what type a variable has.
A named value that can never change, fixed when the program is compiled. In Rust it is written with `const`.
Creating a new variable with the same name as an existing one, which hides the old one from then on. The new one may have a different type.
When a calculation produces a number too big (or too small) for its type, like 300 in a type that only holds 0 to 255.
Rust stopping a program (or one thread of it) on purpose with an error message, because something happened that should be impossible, like reading past the end of an array.
Rust's type `()`, whose only value is also written `()`. It means "no meaningful value" and is what a function returns when it returns nothing.
Rust's rules for memory: every value has exactly one owner (usually a variable), and the value is freed when its owner goes away.
Handing a value's ownership to another variable or function. The old name can no longer be used.
Making a full, independent copy of a value, with `.clone()` in Rust. It can be slow for big values, so Rust makes you ask for it.
A Rust type small and simple enough that assigning it just copies it, like integers or `bool`; the original stays usable.
To use a value through a reference without taking ownership of it. The owner gets full use of it back when the borrow ends.
A Rust reference written `&T` that lets you read a value but not change it. Many may exist at the same time.
A Rust reference written `&mut T` that lets you change the value. Only one may exist at a time, and no shared ones alongside it.
The part of the Rust compiler that checks every reference follows the rules: never outliving its value, and never a writer alongside readers.
To get to the value a reference points at, written with `*` in Rust, as in `*count += 1`.
A borrowed view of a run of neighbouring items in an array, vector or string, stored as a start position plus a length.
Rust's `&str` type: a borrowed view of some text, from a `String` or from text written in quotes.
Rust automatically turning one reference type into another when needed, such as `&String` into `&str` or `&Vec<T>` into `&[T]`.
A Rust struct whose fields have no names, only positions, such as `struct Meters(f64);`.
A Rust struct with no fields at all, such as `struct Marker;`.
A small wrapper type around one value, like `struct Meters(f64)`, used so the compiler won't let you mix it up with other values of the same underlying type.
A Rust block, `impl Type { ... }`, that attaches functions and methods to a type.
A function inside a Rust impl block that has no `self` parameter, called with the type's name, like `String::from` or `Rectangle::new`.
Asking the Rust compiler to write standard code for your type automatically, with `#[derive(...)]` above it, for example to make it printable or comparable.
One of the possible options of an enum, such as `Some` or `None` of `Option`. In Rust each variant can carry its own data.
Covering every possible case. A Rust `match` must be exhaustive, or the program doesn't compile.
In Rust, a description of a value's shape, like `Some(x)` or `(a, b)`, that is checked against values and gives names to their parts.
To unpack a value into its parts with a pattern, as in `let (x, y) = point;`.
In Rust, an extra `if` condition on a match branch (a match guard), checked after the pattern fits. Also short for a lock guard: a value that keeps a lock held until it is dropped.
A pattern that always fits, like `(a, b)` on a pair. A refutable pattern, like `Some(x)`, might not fit.
Rust's standard type for a value that may be missing: either `Some(value)` or `None`. Rust uses it instead of null.
Rust's `let Some(x) = value else { ... };`: keep going with `x` if the pattern fits, otherwise run the else block, which must leave.
Taking the value out of an `Option` or `Result` and panicking if there isn't one. Fine in tests and quick experiments.
Rust's standard type for an operation that can fail: either `Ok(value)` or `Err(error)`. The caller has to deal with both.
How many items a Rust Vec or String has room for before it must grab more memory. It is at least as large as the length.
Rust's standard hash table: it stores values under keys and finds any key almost instantly.
The small set of names every Rust file can use without importing them, like Vec, String, Option and Result. Some libraries offer their own prelude to import in one line.
The `entry` method of Rust's maps: it finds or creates the slot for a key in one step, so you can insert or update without looking the key up twice.
A group of Rust packages developed together that share one Cargo.lock file and one build folder.
A method a Rust trait writes out in full, so every type implementing the trait gets it for free (and may replace it).
Rust's rule that you may implement a trait for a type only if the trait or the type comes from your own crate.
A trait that another trait requires: `trait Pretty: Display` means anything implementing Pretty must also implement Display.
A requirement on a generic type, like `T: Display`, saying which traits it must implement; the code may then use those traits' methods.
A place after a Rust function's signature, starting with `where`, to list trait bounds when they're too long to write inline.
A trait implementation for every type that meets a bound, like `impl<T: Display> ToString for T`.
How Rust compiles generic code: it makes a separate, specialised copy for each concrete type used. Fast to run, but more to compile.
Rust's `::<>` syntax for spelling out a generic type when calling something, as in `parse::<u32>()`.
When a closure uses a variable from the code around it. Rust closures capture by shared reference, mutable reference or by taking ownership.
The three traits closures implement: `FnOnce` (can be called once), `FnMut` (may change what it captured) and `Fn` (only reads it).
A closure written with the `move` keyword, which takes ownership of everything it captures.
A type named inside a trait that each implementation fills in, like `Item` for an iterator's item type.
A method like `map` or `filter` that turns one iterator into another. Adapters do no work until something consumes the items.
In Rust, the stretch of code during which a reference is valid. Lifetime annotations like `'a` describe how the lifetimes of references relate.
Rust's rules for filling in lifetimes you leave out, so most functions taking and returning references need no annotations.
A code example in a Rust documentation comment that `cargo test` also compiles and runs, so the documentation stays correct.
A struct that owns some data and can be used like a pointer to it, cleaning up automatically, such as Box, Rc, String or Vec.
Rust's simplest smart pointer: `Box<T>` puts a value on the heap with a single owner.
Rust's reference-counted pointer: `Rc<T>` lets several owners share one read-only value; it is freed when the last owner goes away.
A Rust container that checks the borrowing rules while the program runs instead of at compile time, panicking if they're broken.
A value used only through a trait, written `dyn Trait`, so the actual type is decided while the program runs. It always sits behind a pointer, like `Box<dyn Trait>`.
A bound like `for<'x> Fn(&'x str)` meaning "for every possible lifetime": the closure must work whatever lifetime each call's input has.
Rust quietly making a new, shorter borrow from an existing `&mut` reference, so passing it to a function doesn't use it up.
Rust 2024's `+ use<...>` syntax on an `impl Trait` return type, listing exactly which generic parameters and lifetimes the hidden type may depend on.
A table the Rust compiler builds for each type used as a trait object, listing where that type's methods are, plus its size and how to drop it.
A pointer that carries extra information next to the address: a length for slices, or a vtable pointer for trait objects. It is two machine words wide.
Choosing which method to run while the program runs, by looking it up in a vtable, instead of fixing the choice at compile time (static dispatch).
A Rust trait whose methods can be called through a vtable, so it can be used as a trait object. Formerly called object safe.
Rust types (Cell, RefCell, Mutex and others) that allow changing a value through a shared reference, keeping it safe some other way.
Breaking a rule the compiler relies on, such as reading freed memory. The program may then do anything at all, including seeming to work until it doesn't.
A thread started with Rust's `thread::scope`, which is guaranteed to finish before the scope ends, so it may borrow local variables.
Rust's thread-safe reference-counted pointer: `Arc<T>` lets several threads share ownership of one value.
Something only one thread can hold at a time, used to keep threads from changing the same data at once. Others trying to take it wait their turn.
Rust marking a Mutex as possibly broken because a thread panicked while holding it; later `lock()` calls return an error you can recover from.
A Rust lock that lets many threads read at once or one thread write, never both.
A one-way pipe between threads or tasks: one side sends values, the other receives them, in order.
In Rust async code, a value standing for work that will finish later. It does nothing until something polls or awaits it.
The part of an async runtime that runs futures: it polls each one and polls it again when it is woken.
The most widely used async runtime for Rust: it runs futures on several threads and provides async networking, timers, channels and locks.
A Rust macro written with `macro_rules!`: rules that match pieces of code and say what code to produce instead.
The kind of code a `macro_rules!` variable matches, such as `expr` (an expression), `ident` (a name) or `ty` (a type).
One piece of Rust code as macros see it: a single word, number or symbol, or a whole group in brackets.
Rules that keep names created inside a macro's output from clashing with names in the code that uses the macro.
Rust's `*const T` and `*mut T`: plain memory addresses with no borrowing rules. Creating one is safe; reading through one requires `unsafe`.
A safe Rust API built on a small amount of unsafe code, designed so that no use of it can cause undefined behaviour.
In Rust, the guarantee that no use of a safe API, however odd, can cause undefined behaviour. An API that breaks this is unsound.
A Rust tool that runs your program step by step, checking every operation, to catch undefined behaviour in unsafe code.
Application binary interface: the low-level agreement on how compiled code passes values and results between functions, such as C's calling convention.
The hidden number inside an enum value that records which variant it is.
Rust storing an enum's discriminant in bit patterns its data can never use, such as the null address for a reference, so `Option<&T>` costs no extra space.
A Rust type that takes no memory at all, such as `()` or a struct with no fields.
A Rust type whose size isn't known at compile time, such as `str`, `[T]` or `dyn Trait`; it can only be used behind a pointer.
A Rust trait the compiler implements automatically for a type when all its fields have it, such as Send and Sync.
A Rust trait with no methods that only states a property of a type, such as Copy, Send or Sync.
Rust's marker trait for types whose values may be moved to another thread.
Rust's marker trait for types whose values may be shared between threads by reference.
A type that can be used wherever another type is expected. In Rust, a longer lifetime is a subtype of a shorter one.
A generic type that keeps its parameter's subtype relationship: `&'static str` can be used where a `&'a str` is expected.
A generic type that reverses its parameter's subtype relationship; function parameters, as in `fn(T)`, are the main example.
A zero-sized marker field that tells the Rust compiler a type acts as if it owns or borrows a `T`, for parameters no real field uses.
Rust's auto trait for types that are safe to move even while pinned; for them `Pin` changes nothing.
A value that contains a pointer to another part of itself, so moving it would leave that pointer aimed at the old location.
Turning a pinned reference to a struct into a pinned reference to one of its fields.
A Rust macro written as ordinary Rust code that runs inside the compiler: it receives code and returns new code.
A procedural macro used as `#[derive(Name)]` that adds new code, usually a trait implementation, next to a struct or enum.
A procedural macro used as `#[name(...)]` on an item, which replaces that item with the code it returns.
Foreign function interface: calling functions written in another language, usually C, or letting other languages call yours.

concepts.name: Programs, source code and the compiler
concepts.summary: What a program is, how Rust's compiler turns the text you write into one, and why its strict checks help you.
concepts.why: Every later lesson writes code and builds it, so it helps to know what happens between typing text and running a program.
concepts.body:
A **program** is a list of instructions for a computer, the way a recipe is a list of steps for a cook. The computer follows them exactly, one after another, and never guesses what you meant.

Programmers write those instructions as text in a **programming language**, such as Rust. That text is called **source code**. It is saved in ordinary text files; Rust files end in `.rs`.

The chip that actually carries out instructions, the processor (or **CPU**), can't read Rust. It only understands **machine code**: long lists of numbers that nobody wants to write by hand.

So Rust comes with a **compiler**: a program that translates your source code into machine code. That translation step is called **compiling**. The result is an **executable**, a file you can run as a program, just like any app on your computer.

While it translates, Rust's compiler also checks your code very strictly. If something is wrong, such as a typo or using a value in a way that could crash, it refuses to build the program and prints a **compile error** that explains the problem. You fix the code and try again.

That strictness is Rust's big idea. The moment the compiler checks and builds your code is called **compile time**; the moment the program actually runs is called **runtime**. Many mistakes that crash programs at runtime in other languages are caught at compile time in Rust, before any user sees them.

You give commands to Rust's tools in a **terminal**: a text window where you type a command, press Enter and read the reply. On macOS it is the Terminal app; on Windows, PowerShell. The next lesson uses it to create and run your first program.

Rust's error messages are unusually helpful. They point at the exact line, say what went wrong and often suggest the fix. Read them to the end: learning Rust is partly learning to have a conversation with the compiler.
takeaways: Source code is the text you write; the compiler translates it into an executable the computer can run
Rust's compiler checks your code strictly and stops with a compile error when something is wrong
Compile time is when code is checked and built; runtime is when the program runs
pitfalls: Skimming past a compile error: the full message usually tells you exactly what to change.

quiz.q: What does a compiler do?
options: Runs your program on a website
Translates source code into a program the computer can run, checking it for errors along the way
quiz.explain: A compiler turns the text you write into machine code, and Rust's compiler also refuses to build code that has mistakes it can detect.

quiz.q: Rust reports a mistake in your code before the program ever runs. When was it caught?
options: When a user clicks a button
quiz.explain: Compile time is when the compiler checks and builds your code, before the program runs.

concepts.name: Cargo and your first program
concepts.summary: Install Rust, create a project with Cargo, and build and run your first program.
concepts.why: Cargo is the tool you use to create, build and run every Rust project, so it is the first one you touch.
concepts.body:
You install Rust with **rustup**, a small installer from rust-lang.org. It puts two important tools on your computer: `rustc`, the compiler from the previous lesson, and **Cargo**. Run `rustup update` now and then to get the newest version.

Cargo is the helper you actually type commands to. It calls the compiler for you and runs your program, so it is a **build tool**. It also downloads code that other people have shared, so it is a **package manager** too.

Type `cargo new hello` in a terminal and Cargo creates a folder called `hello`. That folder is a **package**: one Rust project, with everything needed to build it.

Inside are two files. `src/main.rs` holds your source code. `Cargo.toml` is the package's settings file, called its **manifest**. It names the package and lists its **dependencies**: packages written by other people that your program uses.

The everyday commands, typed inside the `hello` folder:

- `cargo run` compiles your program and then runs it.
- `cargo check` only looks for compile errors, without producing a program. It is much faster, so use it often while you write.
- `cargo build --release` produces a finished, fully speed-tuned executable in `target/release/`.

Without `--release`, Cargo makes a **debug build**: quick to compile and handy while you are still fixing mistakes, but 10 to 50 times slower to run. A **release build** takes longer to compile and runs at full speed. Always use a release build when you measure how fast a program is.

Also standard: `cargo fmt` tidies your code's layout, and `cargo clippy` runs a **linter**, a tool that points out code that works but could be better.

Cargo has already written a tiny program in `src/main.rs`. `fn main() { ... }` is where every Rust program starts: the lines between the curly braces run from top to bottom. `println!("Hello, world!");` prints a line of text in the terminal. A piece of text between double quotation marks is called a **string**, and most lines end with a semicolon.

The `!` in `println!` marks a **macro**: a Rust shortcut that the compiler replaces with longer code before compiling it. Inside the quotation marks, each `{}` is a placeholder that gets filled with a value, in order: `println!("{} + {} = {}", 2, 3, 2 + 3)` prints `2 + 3 = 5`.
takeaways: `cargo new` creates a project, `cargo run` builds and runs it, `cargo check` is the quick error check
`fn main()` is where a program starts; `println!` prints a line, filling each `{}` with a value
Measure speed only with a release build (`cargo build --release`)
pitfalls: Timing a debug build and concluding that Rust is slow.

quiz.q: You are writing code and only want to know whether it compiles. Which command answers fastest?
quiz.explain: cargo check runs all of the compiler's checks but skips producing a program, so it is the quickest feedback.

quiz.q: What does `println!("{} apples and {} pears", 3, 5);` print?
quiz.explain: Each `{}` is filled with the next value in order, so the first gets 3 and the second gets 5.

concepts.name: Variables and mutability
concepts.summary: Store values under names with let, allow changes with mut, and know when to use shadowing and const.
concepts.why: Almost every line of a program stores or reads a value, and Rust's rule that values don't change unless you say so makes programs easier to follow.
concepts.body:
Programs keep track of values: a score, a name, a price. A **variable** is a name for a value, like a label on a box. You create one with `let`: `let score = 10;` stores 10 under the name `score`. To print it, put the name in braces: `println!("{score}")`.

Rust variables are **immutable** by default: once set, the value can't change, and writing `score = 11;` later is a compile error. If you want a variable you can change, say so with `mut`, short for **mutable**: after `let mut score = 10;` the line `score = 11;` is fine. So you can see at a glance which values might change.

Every value has a **data type**, the kind of value it is: a whole number, a decimal number, a piece of text, and so on. The type decides what you can do with it; you can add two numbers, but you can't add a number to a piece of text.

Rust usually works out the type by itself from the value, which is called **type inference**. You can also write the type after a colon, a **type annotation**: `let count: u32 = 0;` says `count` is a `u32`, a whole number that can't be negative. When the compiler can't work the type out, it asks you to add one.

Code between curly braces `{ }` is called a **block**. A variable only exists inside the block where it was created; that stretch of code is its **scope**. After the closing brace, the name can't be used.

**Shadowing** means creating a new variable with the same name as an existing one: `let x = x + 1;`. From that line on, the name means the new variable. Unlike `mut`, this makes a brand-new variable, so it may even have a different type. That is handy for cleaning up a value step by step, such as turning the text `" 42 "` into the number 42.

`const` creates a **constant**: a value fixed forever, worked out at compile time. It always needs a type annotation and, by convention, a name in capitals: `const MAX_USERS: u32 = 1_000;` (the underscore is only for readability). Constants can be written outside `fn main`, so the whole file can use them.

Rust warns about variables you never use. If that is on purpose, start the name with an underscore, as in `_unused`.
takeaways: `let` creates a variable; it can't change unless you write `let mut`
Shadowing makes a new variable with the same name, and it may have a different type
`const` needs a type annotation and is fixed at compile time
pitfalls: Reaching for `mut` when shadowing (a new, cleaned-up variable) would show your intent more clearly.

quiz.q: What is the key difference between `let x = x * 2;` (shadowing) and `x = x * 2;` on a variable made with `let mut x`?
options: Shadowing creates a new variable, which may have a different type
Shadowing changes the original value in place
There is no difference at all
quiz.explain: Shadowing introduces a brand-new variable that reuses the name, so its type may differ; assigning to a `mut` variable must keep the same type.

quiz.q: What happens when you compile `let x = 5; x = 6;`?
options: A compile error, because x is not mutable
quiz.explain: Variables are immutable unless declared with `mut`, and the compiler rejects the assignment.

concepts.name: Scalar and compound types
concepts.summary: Rust's basic types: whole numbers, decimals, true/false and characters, plus tuples and arrays, and converting between them.
concepts.why: Rust never converts numbers for you behind your back, so knowing the basic types saves you from most early compile errors.
concepts.body:
The simplest types hold a single value. They are called **scalar** types, and Rust has four kinds: whole numbers, decimal numbers, true/false values and single characters.

**Integers** are whole numbers such as -3, 0 or 42. In a name like `i32` or `u8`, `i` means it may be negative and `u` means it may not, and the number says how many **bits** (single 0-or-1 digits) it uses. `u8` uses 8 bits, one **byte**: enough for 0 to 255. Sizes go up to `i128`/`u128`; the default is `i32`.

Numbers with a decimal point, like 3.75, are **floating-point numbers**: `f64` (the default) or `f32`. The type `bool` is a **boolean**: either `true` or `false`.

`char` holds one character between single quotation marks, like `'a'`, `'é'` or an emoji: anything listed in **Unicode**, the worldwide catalogue of characters. And `usize` is the integer type for positions and sizes, such as how many items a list holds.

Rust never converts between number types on its own: adding an `i32` to a `u64` is a compile error. You do the **type conversion** yourself. `x as i64` is quick but silently chops off whatever doesn't fit; `u8::try_from(300)` checks first and reports that 300 is too big. Prefer checking when a value might not fit.

Going past the largest value a type can hold is called **overflow**. In a debug build Rust then stops the program with an error message, which is called a **panic**; in a release build the number wraps around. To choose the behaviour yourself, use helpers like `saturating_add`, which stops at the maximum.

A **tuple** groups a fixed number of values that may have different types: `(i32, f64, bool)`. Read the parts with `t.0`, `t.1`, or take them all out at once: `let (a, b, c) = t;`. The empty tuple `()` is called the **unit value** and means "nothing".

An **array** holds a fixed number of values of one type: `[u8; 4]` is four `u8`s, and `[0; 256]` is 256 zeros. An item's position is its **index**, counting from 0, so `arr[0]` is the first item. Asking for `arr[10]` in a four-item array panics instead of reading random data.

A list that can grow is a **vector**, written `vec![1, 2, 3]`; a later lesson covers it. To print tuples, arrays or vectors, use `{:?}` instead of `{}`: it prints values in a form meant for programmers, like `[0, 0, 0]`.
takeaways: The default number types are `i32` and `f64`; `usize` is for positions and sizes
Rust never converts numbers silently: use `as`, or `try_from` when the value might not fit
Overflow panics in debug builds and wraps around in release builds, unless you use `saturating_add` or a similar helper
Tuples group a few values of mixed types; arrays hold a fixed number of one type, counted from index 0
pitfalls: Using `as` to squeeze a big number into a small type and silently getting a wrong value; use `try_from` when it might not fit.

quiz.q: `300_i32` is the number 300 stored as an `i32`. What does `300_i32 as u8` produce?
options: A panic while the program runs
quiz.explain: `as` keeps only what fits in 8 bits: 300 minus 256 is 44, with no error and no panic.

quiz.q: Which type is used for array positions and lengths?
quiz.explain: Positions (indexes) and lengths use `usize`, whose size matches the computer.

concepts.name: Functions and expressions
concepts.summary: Write your own functions with inputs and a result, and learn why almost everything in Rust produces a value.
concepts.why: Functions let you name a piece of work and reuse it, and knowing that Rust blocks produce values explains its most common beginner error.
concepts.body:
A **function** is a named, reusable piece of code, like a recipe you write once and follow whenever you need it. You already know one: `main`. You write your own with `fn`. Running a function is called calling it: you write its name followed by parentheses.

Functions can take inputs. Each input is a **parameter**, written in the parentheses with a name and a type: `fn area(width: f64, height: f64)`. The actual values you pass in when calling, as in `area(2.0, 3.5)`, are the **arguments**.

A function can hand back a result, its **return value**. The result's type goes after an arrow: `-> f64`. Rust always makes you write these types, even though it works out types inside a function on its own, so every function's first line clearly says what goes in and what comes out.

Rust code is built from **expressions**: pieces of code that produce a value, like `2 + 3` or `width * height`. A **statement** is an instruction that does something but produces no value, like `let x = 5;`. Putting a semicolon after an expression turns it into a statement.

A block of code in curly braces produces the value of its last expression, as long as that expression has no semicolon after it. That is how a function returns its result without any special word:

```rust
fn square(x: i32) -> i32 {
    x * x
}
```

Add a semicolon (`x * x;`) and the last line becomes a statement. The block then produces nothing, written `()`, and you get the error "mismatched types: expected `i32`, found `()`". Everyone hits this one; now you will recognise it.

`return` still exists, for leaving a function early, for example when a check at the top fails. It is a **keyword**, a word with a fixed meaning in Rust, like `fn` and `let`. The choices you will write with `if` in the next lesson produce values the same way blocks do.

A function without `->` returns `()`. Function names use lowercase words joined by underscores, like `total_price`, and you may call a function that is written further down the file. When you call a function you must pass every argument it asks for, and two functions can't share a name; give them different names instead.
takeaways: Parameter types and the return type are always written out
A block's value is its last expression, written without a `;`
`return` is for leaving early; a stray `;` on the last line gives "expected …, found ()"
pitfalls: Ending the last line of a function with `;` and getting `expected i32, found ()`.

quiz.q: What does `fn f() -> i32 { 5; }` produce?
options: A compile error: the body produces () instead of an i32
A warning only, and it returns 5
quiz.explain: The semicolon turns `5` into a statement, so the body's value is `()`, which does not match `i32`.

concepts.name: Control flow: if, loop, while, for
concepts.summary: Make decisions with if and else, repeat work with loop, while and for, and count with ranges.
concepts.why: Choosing between actions and repeating them are things every program does, and Rust's versions have a few useful twists.
concepts.body:
Programs often have to choose: if the password is right, let the user in; otherwise, show an error. Code like that is a **conditional**, written with `if` and `else`: `if age >= 18 { ... } else { ... }`. The first block runs only when the condition is true, the `else` block otherwise.

Signs such as `+`, `>=`, `==` (equal) and `!=` (not equal) are called **operators**. In Rust a condition must be a `bool`. Some languages also accept a number and treat 0 as false, but Rust doesn't: `if count { }` won't compile, so write `if count != 0`.

`if` is an expression, so it can produce a value, as long as both **branches** (the two alternative paths) produce the same type: `let size = if n > 100 { "big" } else { "small" };`.

To repeat work you write a **loop**. Each trip through it is one **iteration**. Rust has three kinds:

- `loop { }` repeats forever, until you write `break`. It can also hand back a value: `break 7` makes the whole loop produce 7, handy for "keep trying until it works".
- `while condition { }` repeats as long as the condition stays true.
- `for item in collection { }` goes through each item of a collection, such as an array, one at a time. It is the most common loop, and it can't step past the end by mistake.

Ranges make counting easy: `0..5` counts 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 (the end is left out), `0..=5` includes 5, and `(0..5).rev()` counts down. To loop over a collection and keep using it afterwards, put `&` in front of it: `for x in &items` (a later lesson explains why). If you also need each item's position, use `for (i, x) in items.iter().enumerate()`.

When one loop sits inside another, `break` leaves only the inner one. Give the outer loop a label, such as `'outer: for ...`, and `break 'outer` leaves both; `continue 'outer` skips to its next round.

If you have seen other languages: Rust has no `for (i = 0; i < n; i++)` loop and no `++`. Use ranges, and `count += 1` to add 1 to a `mut` variable.
takeaways: Conditions must be `true` or `false`; numbers are not accepted
`for x in &collection` and ranges like `0..n` cover most counting loops
`loop` can produce a value with `break value`; labels let `break` leave an outer loop
pitfalls: Writing `for x in list` over a vector and then finding `list` can no longer be used; loop over `&list` instead (a later lesson explains why).

quiz.q: How many times does the body of `for i in 0..=3 {}` run?
quiz.explain: `0..=3` is an inclusive range: 0, 1, 2, 3, so four iterations.

quiz.q: What value does `let v = loop { break 7; };` give `v`?
options: It does not compile because loop cannot be assigned
quiz.explain: `loop` is an expression, and `break 7` makes it produce 7.

concepts.name: Ownership and moves
concepts.summary: Every value has one owner; handing it to another variable moves it, and it is cleaned up when its owner's scope ends.
concepts.why: Ownership is how Rust frees memory safely without a garbage collector, and every later lesson builds on it.
concepts.body:
A running program keeps its values in the computer's **memory**, its fast working space. Memory is limited, so a program must give back space it no longer needs. Forget, and it slowly eats all the memory; give space back too early, and it may read garbage and crash.

Many languages use a **garbage collector**: a helper running alongside your program that now and then finds values nothing uses and frees them. It is convenient but costs time while the program runs. Rust has none. Instead the compiler works out, at compile time, exactly when each value can be freed, using rules called **ownership**.

The rules: each value has exactly one **owner**, usually a variable. When the owner's scope ends (the closing `}` of its block), the value is **dropped**: its memory is freed automatically.

Values with a fixed, known size, like numbers, live on **the stack**: a tidy pile where each function's variables are added when it starts and removed when it finishes.

Values whose size can change, like text that grows, live on the **heap**: a large, free-form area where space is handed out as needed. The variable on the stack holds the location of that data.

`String` is Rust's growable text type, kept on the heap; `let s1 = String::from("hello");` makes one from quoted text. Now `let s2 = s1;` does not copy the text. It **moves** ownership to `s2`, and using `s1` afterwards is a compile error (`borrow of moved value`); otherwise both would try to free the same text. Passing a value to a function moves it too, and returning a value moves it out to the caller.

When you really want a second, independent copy, ask for it: `let s3 = s2.clone();`. To **clone** a big value can be slow, so Rust makes you ask out loud, where readers can see it.

Small values that live entirely on the stack, such as integers, floats, `bool`, `char`, and tuples or arrays of these, are **`Copy`** types: assigning one copies it, and the original stays usable. Anything that owns heap data, like `String` or a vector, is not `Copy`.

A variable moved in only one branch of an `if` counts as moved afterwards. Moving values in and out of every function would be tedious, which is why the next lesson introduces borrowing.
takeaways: Each value has one owner and is dropped (freed) when the owner's scope ends
Assigning or passing a value that isn't `Copy` moves it; the old name can't be used afterwards
`.clone()` makes an explicit copy; small stack-only values like integers are `Copy`
pitfalls: Adding `.clone()` everywhere to make compile errors go away, instead of borrowing (next lesson).

quiz.q: After `let v = vec![1, 2]; let w = v;`, what happens if you use `v`?
options: It works, both names share the same vector
It works, w is a separate copy
quiz.explain: A vector is not `Copy`, so the assignment moves ownership to `w` and the compiler rejects later uses of `v`.

quiz.q: Which of these is a `Copy` type?
quiz.explain: A tuple made only of `Copy` types is `Copy`; the others contain heap data and are moved.

concepts.name: References and borrowing
concepts.summary: Let code use a value without taking it, with & and &mut references, and learn the rule: many readers or one writer.
concepts.why: Borrowing is how you use values without moving them around, and its rules are what the Rust compiler checks most often.
concepts.body:
Moving a value into every function that only wants to look at it would be awkward. Instead you can lend it. A **reference** points at a value without owning it, and is written with `&`: `&s` means "a reference to `s`". A function that takes a `&String` can read the text while the caller keeps ownership. Using a value through a reference is called **borrowing**.

To change a value through a reference, both the variable and the reference must be mutable: `let mut s = ...;` and then `add_excl(&mut s);` with `fn add_excl(s: &mut String)`. So `&T` (where `T` stands for any type) is a **shared reference**, for reading, and `&mut T` is a **mutable reference**, for changing.

Rust's central rule: at any moment you may have either any number of shared references to a value, or exactly one mutable reference, never both. Think of a document: many people can read it at once, or one person can edit it, but nobody should be reading while someone is halfway through an edit. The part of the compiler that checks this is the **borrow checker**.

The rule prevents real mistakes. For example, you can't add an item to a vector while holding a reference to one of its items, because adding may move all the items to a new, bigger space and leave your reference pointing at nothing. In many languages that mistake crashes at runtime; in Rust it is a compile error.

A reference must never outlive the value it points to. A function can't return a reference to one of its own **local variables** (variables created inside it), because they are dropped when the function ends. Return the value itself instead.

A borrow lasts only until the reference is used for the last time, not until the end of the block. That is why "take `&v[0]`, print it, then add to `v`" compiles: the borrow ended at the print.

A **method** is a function you call with a dot after a value, like `s.len()`, which gives the length of `s`. The dot follows references for you, so `s.len()` works whether `s` is a `String` or a reference to one. Elsewhere, `*` reaches the value behind a reference, which is called dereferencing: `*count += 1` adds 1 through a `&mut i32`.
takeaways: `&T` borrows for reading, `&mut T` for changing; the owner keeps ownership
Many `&T` or one `&mut T` at a time, never both
A borrow lasts until the reference's last use, not until the end of the block
pitfalls: Holding a reference to a vector's item while adding to the vector; the compiler rejects it because adding may move the items.

quiz.q: Why does Rust reject taking `&mut v` while a `&v[0]` is still used later?
options: Vectors can never be changed through a reference
A mutable borrow and a shared borrow of the same value may not overlap
Only one reference of any kind is allowed
quiz.explain: If the change happened while the shared reference was still in use, it could leave that reference pointing at moved or freed data, so the borrow checker forbids the overlap.

concepts.name: Slices and string slices
concepts.summary: Borrow part of an array, vector or String as a slice (&[T] or &str), and write functions that accept any of them.
concepts.why: A function that takes a slice accepts more kinds of input and never needs to copy it.
concepts.body:
Often you want part of a list or text: the first three scores, or the first word of a sentence. A **slice** lets you borrow a run of items stored side by side, without copying them. Under the hood it is just two things: where the run starts and how long it is. A slice owns nothing, so the borrowing rules apply to it.

You will use two kinds all the time. `&[T]` is a slice of items of type `T`, taken from an array or a vector. `&str` is a **string slice**: a borrowed piece of text, taken from a `String` or written directly between quotation marks.

Taking a slice with a range in square brackets is called **slicing**: `&v[1..3]` is the items at positions 1 and 2, `&v[..2]` the first two, `&v[2..]` everything from position 2 on, and `&v[..]` the whole thing. A range that goes past the end panics.

Text written directly between quotation marks, like `"hello"`, is a **string literal**. Its type is `&'static str`: a slice of text stored inside the program itself, valid for as long as the program runs. (`'static` means "lasts for the whole program"; a later lesson explains these markers.)

The most useful habit concerns function parameters. Prefer `&str` over `&String`, and `&[T]` over `&Vec<T>` (`Vec<T>` is the type of a vector of `T`s). Rust turns a `&String` into a `&str`, and a `&Vec<T>` into a `&[T]`, automatically whenever needed, which is called **deref coercion**. So the slice version accepts everything the other one does, plus string literals and arrays.

Because a slice borrows from its source, the source must stay alive and unchanged while the slice is in use: you can't empty a `String` while still using a `&str` of its first word.

One catch with text. Computers store text as bytes, and Rust uses a system called **UTF-8** to do it: plain English letters take one byte each, but `é` takes two and an emoji four. String slice positions count bytes, not letters, so cutting through the middle of a letter, as in `&"héllo"[0..2]`, panics while the program runs. For text, prefer methods such as `split_whitespace` or `char_indices`, which always give valid positions.

`&mut [T]` is a mutable slice: you can change items in place, for example sort them with `slice.sort()`, but you can't add or remove items.
takeaways: A slice borrows part of a collection: a start plus a length, written `&[T]` or `&str`
Take `&str` and `&[T]` parameters; `&String` and `&Vec` turn into them automatically
String slice positions count bytes, so they must not cut a character in half
pitfalls: Cutting text at a fixed byte position and panicking on letters like `é` that take more than one byte.

quiz.q: Which parameter type accepts a `String` (passed as `&s`), a string literal and a `&str` from elsewhere?
quiz.explain: A `&String` turns into `&str` automatically and literals already are `&str`, so `&str` covers all three.

concepts.name: Structs and methods
concepts.summary: Group related values into your own type with a struct, and attach functions to it in an impl block.
concepts.why: Structs are how you describe the things your program deals with, such as users, orders or rectangles, and impl blocks are where most Rust code lives.
concepts.body:
So far each variable held one value. Real things have several details: a user has a name, an email address and an active flag. A **struct** lets you define your own type that groups named values; each named value is a **field**.

`struct User { name: String, active: bool }` defines the type. To create a value of it, give every field a value: `User { name: String::from("Ana"), active: true }`. Read a field with a dot: `user.name`.

Two shortcuts. If a variable has the same name as a field, write the name once: `User { name, active: true }`. And `User { active: false, ..other }` takes the remaining fields from another `User` (moving any that aren't `Copy`).

A **tuple struct** has fields without names: `struct Meters(f64);`. It is handy as a light wrapper, a **newtype**, that stops you from mixing up `Meters` and `Seconds` even though both hold an `f64`. A **unit struct** such as `struct Marker;` has no fields at all.

You attach functions to a struct in an **impl block** (short for implementation). Functions there that work on one particular value are methods, called with a dot: `rect.area()`. A method's first parameter says how it uses the value:

- `&self` reads it (most methods),
- `&mut self` changes it,
- `self` takes ownership of it, usually to turn it into something else.

Functions in an impl block without a `self` parameter are **associated functions**. You call them with the type's name and `::`, as in `Rectangle::new(3, 4)`. By convention, an associated function that creates a new value is called `new`; a function with that job is called a **constructor**. Inside the block, `Self` is a short name for the type itself.

Fields can't be used from other parts of a bigger program unless they are marked `pub` (public). Keeping fields private and offering methods lets a struct protect its rules, such as "width is never negative".

`#[derive(Debug)]` written above a struct asks the compiler to **derive** (write for you) the code that prints it with `{:?}`, or spread over several lines with `{:#?}`.

Method calls borrow for you: `rect.area()` is turned into `Rectangle::area(&rect)` automatically, so you rarely write `&` when calling a method.
takeaways: Methods take `&self`, `&mut self` or `self` depending on how they use the value
Associated functions like `new` have no `self` and are called as `Type::new(...)`
Tuple structs make cheap newtypes; `#[derive(Debug)]` makes a struct printable with `{:?}`
pitfalls: Taking `self` in a method that only reads, which uses up the caller's value.

quiz.q: A method should change the struct, and the caller must keep using it afterwards. Which first parameter fits?
quiz.explain: `&mut self` borrows mutably, so the method can change fields and the caller keeps ownership.

concepts.name: Enums and match
concepts.summary: Describe a value that is one of several options, each with its own data, and handle every option with match.
concepts.why: Enums plus match let the compiler check that you handled every case, which rules out a whole kind of mistake.
concepts.body:
Some values are always one of a fixed set of options: a traffic light is red, yellow or green; a payment is pending, paid or refunded. An **enum** (short for enumeration) defines a type whose value is exactly one of several **variants**. In Rust each variant can also carry its own data: nothing, a few unnamed values, or named fields.

```rust
enum Shape {
    Circle { radius: f64 },
    Rect(f64, f64),
    Empty,
}
```

You create a value with `Shape::Rect(2.0, 3.0)`, and you can add methods in an impl block, just as with structs.

**`match`** compares a value against a list of **patterns**, descriptions of the shapes a value might have, top to bottom, and runs the code of the first one that fits. Each pattern with its code is one branch of the `match`. A pattern can also pull out a variant's data and give it names, as `Shape::Rect(w, h)` does. Checking values against shapes like this is called **pattern matching**.

`match` is **exhaustive**: if you forget a variant, the program doesn't compile. That is a big deal in practice. When you add a variant later, the compiler lists every `match` that now has to handle it.

The pattern `_` matches anything and works as a catch-all. Use it deliberately, because it also silences those helpful "you forgot a variant" errors when new variants are added.

`match` is an expression, so every branch must produce the same type, and you can store the result in a variable. Branches are separated by commas; a branch can use a `{ ... }` block to run several statements.

When you match on a reference (`match &shape`), the names in the patterns become references to the data inside, so you can look at a value without moving it.

This way of modelling data is used everywhere in Rust: messages between parts of a program, the possible states of something (an order that is pending, paid or shipped), and the standard `Option` and `Result` types you will meet next.
takeaways: Each enum variant can carry different data
`match` is exhaustive: every variant must be handled
Avoid `_` catch-alls where you want the compiler to point out new variants
pitfalls: Using a struct with many maybe-empty fields plus a `kind` text field, where an enum would make impossible combinations impossible to write.

quiz.q: You add a variant `Triangle` to `Shape`. What happens to an existing `match` that lists every variant and has no `_` branch?
options: It silently skips Triangle while running
It panics when it sees a Triangle
It fails to compile until Triangle is handled
It uses the first branch for Triangle
quiz.explain: `match` must be exhaustive, so the compiler reports the missing `Triangle` branch.

concepts.name: Option, if let and let-else
concepts.summary: Represent a value that might be missing with Option<T>, and get at it with match, if let, let-else and helper methods.
concepts.why: Rust has no null; Option is how Rust code says "there might be nothing here", so you will use it constantly.
concepts.body:
Sometimes a value may be missing: looking up a user who doesn't exist, or asking for the first item of an empty list. Many languages use a special value called **null** to mean "nothing here", and forgetting to check for it is one of the most common causes of crashes. Rust has no null.

Instead, a value that may be missing has the type **`Option<T>`**: a standard enum with two variants, `Some(T)`, which holds a value of type `T`, and `None`. Because `Option<i32>` and `i32` are different types, you can't accidentally use a maybe-missing number as if it were there; the compiler makes you deal with `None` first.

You will meet `Option` everywhere: `v.get(i)` (the item at position `i`, if there is one), `s.find('x')` (where `x` first appears, if it does) and many more return one.

Ways to get at the value, from most to least explicit:

- `match opt { Some(x) => ..., None => ... }` handles both possibilities.
- `if let Some(x) = opt { ... }` runs code only when there is a value, optionally with an `else`.
- `let Some(x) = opt else { return; };` is called **let-else**. It gives you `x` for the rest of the function, and its `else` block must leave (with `return`, `break`, `continue` or a panic), because otherwise there would be no `x` to carry on with.
- Helper methods: `opt.unwrap_or(0)` gives the value or 0, and `opt.map(|x| x * 2)` changes the value if there is one. `|x| x * 2` is a tiny unnamed function, a closure; a later lesson covers them.

`unwrap()` gives the value or panics on `None`; `expect("message")` does the same with your own message. They are fine in quick experiments and tests, or when you are certain a value exists, but not for input that can really be missing.

Rust 2024 lets you add more conditions to an `if let` with `&&`: `if let Some(u) = user && u.active { ... }`.

To look inside an `Option<String>` without moving the `String` out of it, use `opt.as_deref()`, which gives an `Option<&str>`, or match on `&opt`.
takeaways: `Option<T>` replaces null; the compiler makes you handle `None`
`if let` for one case, `let ... else` to leave early, helpers like `map` and `unwrap_or` for quick changes
`unwrap` and `expect` panic on `None`; keep them for tests and values you are certain exist
pitfalls: Calling `.unwrap()` on text a user typed and crashing on the first missing value.

quiz.q: What does `Some(3).map(|x| x + 1).unwrap_or(0)` return?
quiz.explain: `map` turns `Some(3)` into `Some(4)`, and `unwrap_or` takes out the 4 because the value is not `None`.

quiz.q: What must the `else` block of `let Some(x) = opt else { ... };` do?
options: Leave, for example with return, break or a panic
quiz.explain: Code after a let-else uses `x`, so the else branch is not allowed to carry on without one.

concepts.name: Patterns and destructuring
concepts.summary: Use patterns everywhere: take apart structs and tuples, add extra conditions, match ranges of values, and name matches with @.
concepts.why: Patterns appear in let, match, loops and function parameters; using them well makes Rust code short and clear.
concepts.body:
A **pattern** describes the shape of a value and gives names to its parts. You have used patterns in `match` and `if let`, but they also work in `let`, in `for` loops, in `while let` (a loop that repeats while the pattern fits) and in function parameters.

Taking a value apart into named pieces with a pattern is called **destructuring**:

- Tuples: `let (x, y) = point;`.
- Structs: `let User { name, age, .. } = user;` where `..` skips the other fields.
- A slice: `match xs { [] => ..., [one] => ..., [first, .., last] => ... }`.
- Function parameters: `fn dist(&(x, y): &(f64, f64))`.

Inside a `match`, `|` means "or" (`1 | 2 => ...`), and ranges match a span of values (`'a'..='z'` or `0..=9`).

A **match guard** adds an extra condition with `if`: `Some(n) if n > 100 => ...`. The guard is checked after the pattern fits; if it is false, Rust tries the next branch. The compiler ignores guards when checking that every possibility is handled, so you usually still need a final catch-all branch.

`@` names a value while also testing it against a pattern: `n @ 1..=9 => println!("digit {n}")`.

`_` ignores one value without naming it; a name starting with an underscore, like `_name`, keeps the value but silences the unused warning; `..` ignores all the rest.

Patterns in a plain `let` must be **irrefutable**: they always fit, like taking apart a pair. Patterns that might not fit, like `Some(x)`, need `if let`, `while let`, `let ... else` or `match`.

Matching on a reference gives you references to the parts, so `match &user` lets you look at fields without moving them. The older keywords `ref` and `ref mut` are only needed in the rare situations this doesn't cover.
takeaways: Patterns work in `let`, `match`, `if let`, `while let`, `for` and function parameters
Use `|`, ranges, `..`, guards and `@` to say exactly what should match
`let` needs patterns that always fit; ones that may fail need `if let`, `let-else` or `match`
pitfalls: Expecting the compiler to count branches with guards as covering every possibility; it never does.

quiz.q: Given `match n { x if x < 0 => "neg", 0 => "zero" }` on an i32, why does it fail to compile?
options: Guards are not allowed with integers
Positive numbers are not covered, and guards don't count when checking coverage
quiz.explain: Positive values match no branch; the compiler requires a catch-all such as `_ => "pos"`.

concepts.name: Result and the ? operator
concepts.summary: Return Result<T, E> from functions that can fail, pass errors up with ?, and keep panics for programming mistakes.
concepts.why: Reading a file, turning text into a number, talking over the network: anything that can fail returns a Result, so handling it fluently is the core of practical Rust.
concepts.body:
Rust separates two kinds of failure. **Unrecoverable** errors are programming mistakes, such as reading past the end of a list or reaching a state the code assumed was impossible. They cause a `panic!`, which stops the running program. **Recoverable** errors, like a missing file or bad input, are ordinary values of type **`Result<T, E>`**, an enum with `Ok(T)` and `Err(E)`.

You can `match` on a `Result`, but the idiomatic way to pass errors up is the **`?` operator**. Inside a function that returns a `Result`, `let text = fs::read_to_string(path)?;` means: if `Ok`, unwrap the value; if `Err`, return it from the current function immediately. Before returning, `?` also converts the error into your function's error type, using that type's `From` conversion. So a function returning `Result<T, MyError>` can use `?` on any error that `MyError` knows how to convert from (the standard-traits lesson shows how to write `From`). `?` also works on `Option` in functions returning `Option`.

`main` can return `Result<(), E>` where `E: Debug`; returning `Err` prints the error and ends the program with a code that tells whoever started it that it failed. A convenient quick version is `fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>>`: a box that can hold any error type from the **standard library**, the code that ships with Rust (boxes and `dyn` come later).

Useful methods: `map_err` to change the error type, `ok()` to turn it into an `Option`, `unwrap_or_else`, `and_then`, and `is_ok()`/`is_err()`. `unwrap()` and `expect()` panic on `Err`.

`Result` is marked `#[must_use]`, so ignoring one produces a warning. If you really do not care, write `let _ = do_thing();` to show it was deliberate.

A good rule: a **library** (code written for other programs to use) returns `Result` and lets the caller decide; only the application at the top decides whether to print the error, try again or exit.
takeaways: Panics are for programming mistakes; `Result` is for failures the caller should handle
`?` returns early on `Err` and converts the error with `From`
`main` can return `Result` to use `?` at the top level
pitfalls: Using `.unwrap()` on every `Result` inside a library, turning recoverable errors into crashes.

quiz.q: In `fn load() -> Result<Config, AppError>`, what lets `std::fs::read_to_string(p)?` compile?
options: Nothing; ? only works with matching error types
quiz.explain: `?` calls `From::from` on the error, so it needs a `From<io::Error>` impl for `AppError`.

quiz.q: What does `?` do when applied to `Ok(v)`?
quiz.explain: On success `?` simply unwraps the value; it only returns early on `Err`.

concepts.name: Vectors
concepts.summary: Store a growable list in Vec<T>: create, push, index safely, iterate, and understand capacity.
concepts.why: Vec is Rust's everyday list; most data your programs work with will pass through one.
concepts.body:
**`Vec<T>`** is a growable, heap-allocated array of `T`. Create one with `Vec::new()`, `Vec::with_capacity(n)` when you know roughly how many elements are coming, or the `vec![1, 2, 3]` macro.

Adding and removing: `push`, `pop` (returns `Option<T>`), `insert(i, x)`, `remove(i)` (shifts every later element, so it is slow on long vectors), `swap_remove(i)` (fast, but changes the order), `extend`, `truncate`, `clear`, `retain(|x| ...)` to filter in place, and `dedup` after a `sort`.

Reading: `v[i]` panics if out of bounds, while `v.get(i)` returns an `Option<&T>`. Use `get` when the index comes from outside your control.

Because a `Vec<T>` derefs to a slice `[T]`, every slice method is available: `len`, `is_empty`, `contains`, `iter`, `sort`, `sort_by_key`, `binary_search`, `windows`, `chunks`, `first`, `last`, `split_at`, and more. So you can pass `&v` wherever a `&[T]` is expected.

Iteration comes in three flavours:

- `for x in &v` borrows each element (`&T`),
- `for x in &mut v` gives `&mut T` for in-place edits,
- `for x in v` consumes the vector and yields owned `T`.

Under the hood a `Vec` is three numbers: a **pointer** (the address on the heap where its items start), a **length** (how many items it holds) and a **capacity** (how many fit before it needs more room). When `len` reaches `capacity`, the next push grabs a new block of heap memory (roughly twice as big) and moves all the items there. That is why the borrow checker forbids holding a reference into a vector across a `push`. `shrink_to_fit` releases spare capacity.

To store values of different types in one `Vec`, wrap them in an enum with one variant per type (a later lesson shows another way, trait objects).
takeaways: Use `vec![]` or `Vec::with_capacity`; `get` returns `Option`, `[]` panics
A `Vec` derefs to a slice, so all slice methods apply
`&v`, `&mut v` and `v` in a `for` loop borrow, mutably borrow, or consume
pitfalls: Calling `remove(0)` again and again on a large Vec, which shifts every item each time; `VecDeque` removes from the front quickly.

quiz.q: Why can't you keep `let first = &v[0];` alive across `v.push(9)`?
options: push may move the items to new memory and leave `first` pointing at freed memory
quiz.explain: Reallocation moves the elements, so the borrow checker forbids the overlapping shared and mutable borrows.

concepts.name: String and UTF-8 text
concepts.summary: Work with owned String and borrowed &str, build and format text, and handle UTF-8 correctly.
concepts.why: Text handling is where newcomers trip most, because Rust strings are always valid UTF-8 and never indexed by position.
concepts.body:
Rust has two main string types. **`String`** is owned, growable text stored on the heap. **`&str`** is a borrowed slice of UTF-8 text, from a `String` or a string literal. Use `&str` for parameters, `String` when you need to own or build text. Convert with `s.as_str()` / `&s` one way and `s.to_string()`, `String::from(s)` or `s.to_owned()` the other.

Building text: `push_str`, `push` (one `char`), `+` (which uses up the left-hand `String`: `s1 + &s2`), and the `format!` macro, which is usually the clearest. `write!` into a `String` works too via `std::fmt::Write`.

Both types are guaranteed **valid UTF-8**. A character may take 1 to 4 bytes, so:

- `s.len()` is the length in **bytes**, not characters.
- `s[0]` does not compile. There is no quick way to jump to the n-th character; Rust would have to walk the text from the start.
- `s.chars()` goes through the characters (as `char`s), `s.bytes()` goes through the bytes, and `s.char_indices()` gives valid byte offsets for slicing.

Common operations: `trim`, `split`, `split_whitespace`, `lines`, `contains`, `starts_with`, `strip_prefix`, `replace`, `to_lowercase`, `parse::<T>()`, `repeat`, and `chars().rev().collect::<String>()` to reverse.

What users perceive as a character (a grapheme, e.g. an emoji with a skin-tone modifier) can be several `char`s; for that you need the `unicode-segmentation` crate, a shared package from `crates.io`.

Other string types exist for good reasons: `OsString`/`OsStr` for text that comes from the operating system, such as file names, which may not be valid UTF-8; `PathBuf`/`Path` for file paths; and `CString`/`CStr` for exchanging text with code written in C. Do not force those through `String`.
takeaways: `String` owns text, `&str` borrows it; take `&str` parameters
`len()` counts bytes; iterate with `chars()` and slice at `char_indices` offsets
`format!` is the clearest way to build strings
pitfalls: Assuming `s.len()` is the number of characters for non-ASCII text.

quiz.q: What is `"héllo".len()`?
quiz.explain: `len` counts UTF-8 bytes and `é` takes two bytes, so the result is 6.

concepts.name: HashMap and the entry API
concepts.summary: Store key-value pairs in HashMap, update counts and groups with the entry API, and know when to use BTreeMap or HashSet.
concepts.why: Maps are the second most used collection, and the entry API is the idiomatic way to update them.
concepts.body:
A **`HashMap<K, V>`** stores values of type `V` under keys of type `K`, the way a phone book stores numbers under names. It finds any key almost instantly by turning the key into a number, its **hash**, that says where to look.

It is not in the **prelude** (the small set of names every Rust file can use without asking), so **import** it first: `use std::collections::HashMap;`. Keys must be comparable for equality and hashable; for your own types, `#[derive(PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]` is enough.

Basic operations: `insert(k, v)` returns the previous value as an `Option`; `get(&k)` returns `Option<&V>`; `get_mut`, `remove`, `contains_key`, `len`. You can build a map from a sequence of pairs with `.collect()` (see the iterators lesson) or from an array with `HashMap::from([(k, v), ...])`.

Inserting moves owned keys and values into the map. Lookups take a borrowed form, so a `HashMap<String, u32>` can be searched with a `&str`: `scores.get("ann")`.

The **entry API** (the `entry` method and its helpers) handles "insert or update" in one lookup, avoiding the borrow-checker trouble of a `get` followed by `insert`:

- `*map.entry(word).or_insert(0) += 1;` counts occurrences.
- `map.entry(key).or_default().push(item);` groups items into `Vec`s.
- `or_insert_with(|| expensive())` computes the default only when it is needed; `and_modify(|v| ...)` updates an existing value.

Iteration order of a `HashMap` is **unspecified** and changes between runs, because the default hashing (SipHash) starts from a random number on each run. That stops attackers from choosing keys that make the map slow. If you need sorted keys, use **`BTreeMap`**, which keeps keys in order and can hand you all keys within a range. For raw speed on trusted keys, crates like `rustc-hash` or `ahash` provide faster hashers.

The companion sets are `HashSet<T>` and `BTreeSet<T>`, with `insert` returning `false` for duplicates and operations like `intersection` and `union`. `VecDeque` (fast to add or remove at both ends) and `BinaryHeap` (always hands out the largest item first) round out the standard collections.
takeaways: Import `HashMap` from `std::collections`; keys need `Eq + Hash`
Use `entry().or_insert()` / `or_default()` for counting and grouping
HashMap order is random; use `BTreeMap` when order matters
pitfalls: Relying on HashMap iteration order in output or tests.

quiz.q: What is the idiomatic way to increment a counter for `word` in a `HashMap<String, u32>`?
quiz.explain: The entry API finds or creates the slot in one lookup and gives a `&mut u32` to increment.

concepts.name: Modules, crates and packages
concepts.summary: Organise code into modules and files, control visibility with pub, and add dependencies in `Cargo.toml`.
concepts.why: Every project beyond one file needs modules, and every real project depends on crates from `crates.io`.
concepts.body:
A **package** is what `cargo new` creates: a `Cargo.toml` plus one or more **crates**. A crate is one unit the compiler builds: either a **binary** crate, a program you can run, starting from `src/main.rs`, or a **library** crate, code for other programs to use, starting from `src/lib.rs`. A package can have both; the binary then uses the library by its package name.

Inside a crate, code is organised into a tree of **modules**: named sections of code, usually one per file. `mod parser;` in `main.rs` or `lib.rs` tells the compiler to load `src/parser.rs` (or `src/parser/mod.rs`). Modules inside `parser` live in the folder `src/parser/`. You can also write a module directly in a file: `mod tests { ... }`.

Everything is **private by default** to its module (and that module's children). Mark items `pub` to expose them; `pub(crate)` exposes within the crate only. For structs, each field needs its own `pub`; for enums, making the enum `pub` makes all variants public.

Paths: `crate::parser::parse` is absolute from the crate root, `super::` goes up one level, `self::` is the current module. `use` brings names into scope (it **imports** them); idiomatic style imports the parent module for functions (`use std::fs;` then `fs::read`) and the item itself for types (`use std::collections::HashMap;`). `pub use` re-exports a name, so the **API** your crate offers (the set of items other code may use) can be simpler than your file layout.

**Dependencies** go in `Cargo.toml` under `[dependencies]`, e.g. `serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }`, or simply run `cargo add serde --features derive`. Versions follow **semantic versioning**: in 1.4.2, the first number changes only for updates that may break your code. So the requirement `"1.4"` means at least 1.4.0 and below 2.0.0. `Cargo.lock` is a **lock file**: it lists the exact version of every dependency used. Keep it with your source code for applications. `[dev-dependencies]` are only for tests and examples. Large projects group crates in a Cargo **workspace** that shares one lock file and one `target/` folder.
takeaways: A package holds crates; a crate is a tree of modules rooted at main.rs or lib.rs
Items and struct fields are private unless marked `pub`
`cargo add` and `[dependencies]` pull crates from `crates.io` using semantic version ranges
pitfalls: Writing `mod foo;` in every file that uses `foo`; declare a module once, then `use` it elsewhere.

quiz.q: A struct is `pub` but its fields are not. What can code in another module do?
options: Construct it with a struct literal
Use it, but not access or set its private fields directly
Nothing; the struct is still private
quiz.explain: Field privacy is separate from type privacy, so outside code needs public methods such as `new` to create or inspect it.

quiz.q: What does the dependency requirement `rand = "0.8.5"` allow?
quiz.explain: Cargo's caret semantics treat the leftmost non-zero component as the major version, so 0.8.x upgrades are allowed but not 0.9.

concepts.name: Traits
concepts.summary: Define shared behaviour with traits, implement them for your types, and use default methods and impl Trait parameters.
concepts.why: Traits let many different types share the same behaviour, so one function can work with all of them; Rust's own built-in code is built on them.
concepts.body:
A **trait** is a named set of methods that types can promise to provide. Implementing a trait for a type means writing those methods for it. You write `trait Summary { fn summarize(&self) -> String; }` and then `impl Summary for Article { ... }` for each type.

Traits can provide **default methods** that implementing types get for free and may replace with their own version. A default method can call the required ones, so a trait can ask for one small method and offer many on top. This is exactly how Rust's `Iterator` trait works (a later lesson): implement `next`, and you get `map`, `filter`, `sum` and dozens more.

To accept "anything that implements `Summary`", the simplest way to write it is `fn notify(item: &impl Summary)`. In return position, `fn make() -> impl Summary` returns some concrete type the caller cannot name. Both are resolved at compile time, with no runtime cost.

The **orphan rule** says you can implement a trait for a type only if the trait or the type is defined in your own crate (your project). You can implement your trait for `Vec<T>`, or `Display` for your struct, but not `Display` for `Vec<T>`. The usual workaround is a newtype wrapper.

Traits can require other traits (**supertraits**): `trait Pretty: std::fmt::Display { ... }` means implementors must also implement `Display`, and default methods may use `to_string()`.

To call a trait method, the trait must be in scope. If `x.summarize()` mysteriously fails with "method not found", you probably forgot `use crate::Summary;`. Many libraries offer a `prelude` you can import in one line for this reason.

Since Rust 1.75, traits can also contain `-> impl Trait` methods and `async fn` (see the async lesson).
takeaways: A trait lists required methods and may supply default ones
`&impl Trait` parameters and `-> impl Trait` returns are static and zero-cost
Orphan rule: you own the trait or the type; bring traits into scope to call their methods
pitfalls: Forgetting to `use` a trait and wondering why its method does not exist.

quiz.q: Which impl is forbidden by the orphan rule in your own crate?
quiz.explain: Both `Display` and `Vec` come from the standard library, so neither is local to your crate.

concepts.name: Generics and trait bounds
concepts.summary: Write functions and types over any T, constrain T with trait bounds and where clauses, and know what monomorphization costs.
concepts.why: Generics let one function or type work for many types at full speed, and you will read them in nearly every signature in Rust's documentation.
concepts.body:
**Generics** let you write code once for many types. In `fn largest<T: PartialOrd>(items: &[T]) -> &T`, `T` is a placeholder for a type, filled in by each caller, so the function works for slices of integers, of floats or of strings. Structs and enums can be generic too: `struct Pair<T> { a: T, b: T }`, and of course `Vec<T>`, `Option<T>` and `Result<T, E>`.

Inside a generic function you can only do what the **trait bounds** promise. Without `T: PartialOrd` you cannot compare with `>`; without `T: Clone` you cannot call `.clone()`. The compiler checks the generic body once against the bounds, so errors appear where the function is written, not deep inside one particular use of it.

Bounds can be written right after the name (`T: Display + Clone`) or in a **`where` clause**, which reads better when there are several:

```rust
fn report<K, V>(map: &HashMap<K, V>) where K: Display + Eq + Hash, V: Debug { }
```

`impl` blocks can be generic (`impl<T> Pair<T> { }`) or conditional: `impl<T: Display> Pair<T> { fn show(&self) }` adds methods only when `T` qualifies. A **blanket impl** like `impl<T: Display> ToString for T` gives a trait to every type meeting a bound.

Rust compiles generics by **monomorphization**: it generates a specialised copy for each concrete type used. That makes them as fast as hand-written code, at the cost of longer compiling and a bigger executable. When that matters, or when you need a collection of mixed types, trait objects (`dyn Trait`, a later lesson) trade a little speed for one shared copy.

`impl Trait` in argument position is shorthand for an anonymous generic parameter. Use a named `T` when you need to mention the type twice or let callers specify it with the **turbofish** `::<>`: `parse::<u32>()`, `collect::<Vec<_>>()`.

Generics also accept **const parameters**: `fn first<T, const N: usize>(arr: [T; N])`.
takeaways: Trait bounds define what a generic body is allowed to do with `T`
Use `where` clauses for long bounds; conditional `impl` blocks add methods per bound
Generics are monomorphized: zero runtime cost, more compile time and code size
pitfalls: Adding bounds to a struct definition instead of only to the impl blocks that need them.

quiz.q: Why does `fn max<T>(a: T, b: T) -> T { if a > b { a } else { b } }` fail to compile?
options: a and b are moved twice
T has no PartialOrd bound, so `>` is not known to exist
quiz.explain: Generic bodies may only use operations guaranteed by bounds; comparison needs `T: PartialOrd`.

concepts.name: Derive and the standard traits
concepts.summary: Know the standard traits for printing, copying, comparing, hashing, defaults and conversions, and when to derive or write them.
concepts.why: These traits decide whether your types can be printed, compared, hashed, copied or converted, so every type you write needs the right set.
concepts.body:
Rust's standard library (the code that ships with Rust) defines a set of traits that nearly every type should consider. Most can be generated with **`#[derive(...)]`**, which implements them field by field (so each field must implement the trait too).

- `Debug`: `{:?}` formatting for developers. Derive it on almost everything.
- `Clone`: explicit `.clone()`. `Copy`: implicit bitwise copy on assignment; only for small types whose fields are all `Copy`, and it requires `Clone`.
- `PartialEq`/`Eq`: `==`. `Eq` promises equality is reflexive, which floats break (`NaN != NaN`), so `f64` is only `PartialEq`.
- `PartialOrd`/`Ord`: `<`, sorting, `max`. Derived ordering compares fields in declaration order, and enum variants in declaration order.
- `Hash`: needed for `HashMap` keys, together with `Eq`. Keep it consistent with `PartialEq`: equal values must hash equally.
- `Default`: `T::default()` and `..Default::default()` when creating a struct. Enums can derive it by marking one variant `#[default]`.

Some must be written by hand:

- **`Display`**: user-facing `{}` formatting. Implement `fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter) -> fmt::Result` using `write!`. It also gives you `.to_string()` for free.
- **`From<T>`**: infallible conversion. Implementing `From<A> for B` automatically provides `Into<B> for A`, so implement `From`, and let your functions accept `impl Into<B>` when convenient. `TryFrom` is the fallible version.

Other traits you will see in signatures: `AsRef<str>` (cheap reference conversion), `Deref`, `Drop` (custom cleanup when a value goes out of scope), `Iterator` and `IntoIterator`, `Send`/`Sync` for sharing values between threads (covered later), and `FromStr`, which powers `str::parse`.
takeaways: Derive `Debug`, `Clone`, `PartialEq` (and friends) unless you have a reason not to
`Copy` only for small plain-data types; `Eq` and `Hash` must agree with `PartialEq`
Implement `Display` for user-facing output and `From` for conversions; you get `to_string` and `Into` free
pitfalls: Implementing `Into` directly instead of `From`, which loses the blanket conversion.

quiz.q: Why can't you derive `Eq` on a struct containing an `f64` field?
options: f64 does not implement Eq because NaN != NaN
Eq cannot be derived at all
quiz.explain: `Eq` requires reflexive equality, which floating-point NaN violates, so `f64` only implements `PartialEq`.

quiz.q: You implement `From<Celsius> for Kelvin`. What else do you get automatically?
quiz.explain: A blanket impl in std provides `Into<U> for T` whenever `U: From<T>`.

concepts.name: Closures
concepts.summary: Write small unnamed functions that capture variables around them, understand Fn, FnMut and FnOnce, and use move closures.
concepts.why: Closures are how you hand a small piece of behaviour to other code, such as how to sort or what to do with each item, and their rules follow directly from ownership.
concepts.body:
A **closure** is a small function without a name that can **capture** (use) variables from the scope where it is written: `let add = |a, b| a + b;` or with a block body `|x: i32| -> i32 { x * factor }`. Parameter and return types are usually inferred from the first use.

Closures capture in the least demanding way their body allows: by shared reference if they only read a variable, by mutable reference if they change it, or by taking ownership if they move it out. Borrowing rules apply to those captures, so a closure holding `&mut count` blocks other uses of `count` while it is alive.

The capture mode decides which **Fn trait** the closure implements:

- `FnOnce`: can be called at least once; it may consume captured values. Every closure implements it.
- `FnMut`: can be called repeatedly and may change what it captured.
- `Fn`: can be called repeatedly through a shared reference; it only reads captures.

A function that accepts a closure asks for the most permissive bound that works for it: `Option::map` takes `FnOnce` because it calls the closure once, `Iterator::for_each` takes `FnMut`, and code that may call it many times through `&`, or from several threads at once, takes `Fn`.

The **`move`** keyword makes a closure take ownership of everything it captures, even if the body only reads it. You need it when the closure outlives the current scope: returning a closure, or handing it to another thread (covered later). Moving a `Copy` value copies it; to move a clone and keep the original, clone into a new variable first.

To accept a closure, use generics (`fn apply<F: Fn(i32) -> i32>(f: F)`), and to return one, `-> impl Fn(i32) -> i32`.
