Every closure has its own type, so to store different closures together, put them in boxes: `Vec<Box<dyn Fn(i32) -> i32>>` (boxes and `dyn` are covered later). Plain `fn` items also implement all three traits, so you can pass a function name wherever a closure is expected.
takeaways: Closures capture by reference, mutable reference or value, as needed by the body
`Fn` ⊂ `FnMut` ⊂ `FnOnce`: callers ask for the weakest bound they can
Use `move` when the closure must outlive the scope that created it
pitfalls: Forgetting `move` on a closure passed to `thread::spawn` and getting a 'may outlive borrowed value' error.

quiz.q: A closure pushes into a captured `Vec`. Which is the most specific trait it implements?
quiz.explain: Mutating a capture requires a mutable borrow, so the closure is `FnMut` (and therefore also `FnOnce`) but not `Fn`.

concepts.name: Iterators
concepts.summary: Chain lazy iterator adapters like map, filter and enumerate, finish with collect, sum or fold, and implement Iterator.
concepts.why: Iterator chains are the usual way to work through collections in Rust, and they compile to code as fast as hand-written loops.
concepts.body:
An **iterator** hands out items one at a time. In Rust it is anything implementing `trait Iterator { type Item; fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item>; }`. Each call to `next` yields `Some(item)` until it returns `None`. `Item` is an **associated type**, a type named inside a trait: each iterator has exactly one item type.

Collections give you three iterators: `iter()` yields `&T`, `iter_mut()` yields `&mut T`, and `into_iter()` yields owned `T`, consuming the collection. A `for` loop calls `into_iter()` on whatever you give it, which is why `for x in &v` yields references.

**Adapters** turn an iterator into another iterator: `map`, `filter`, `filter_map`, `enumerate`, `zip`, `chain`, `take`, `skip`, `take_while`, `flat_map`, `rev`, `peekable`, `windows` on slices. Adapters are **lazy**: they do no work until something asks for items. A `map` with no consumer does nothing (and the compiler warns).

**Consumers** drive the iteration: `collect`, `sum`, `count`, `min`/`max`, `max_by_key`, `fold`, `any`, `all`, `find`, `position`, `for_each`, `last`.

`collect` is generic over its output: it can build a `Vec`, `String`, `HashMap`, `HashSet`, and even a `Result<Vec<T>, E>` from an iterator of `Result`s, stopping at the first error. Tell it what you want with a type annotation or turbofish: `collect::<Vec<_>>()`.

The compiler merges the small steps of a chain together, so it usually becomes the same machine code as a hand-written loop, often without the checks that each position is in range. Prefer chains for transforming data; use a plain `for` loop when the body has complicated `if`s, `break`s or does other work, like printing.

To make your own type usable as an iterator, implement `next`; all adapters come with the trait. Implement `IntoIterator` for your collection so it works in `for` loops.
takeaways: Implement `next` and you get every adapter for free
Adapters are lazy; consumers like `collect`, `sum` and `for` drive them
`collect` can build any `FromIterator` type, including `Result<Vec<_>, E>`
pitfalls: Calling `.map(...)` only for its effects (like printing) with nothing consuming the items, so nothing runs.

quiz.q: What does `v.iter().map(|x| println!("{x}"));` print?
options: Nothing, because the iterator is never consumed
quiz.explain: Adapters are lazy; without a consumer such as `for_each` or `collect`, the closure never runs (the compiler warns).

quiz.q: Which call yields owned `String`s from a `Vec<String>` and consumes the vector?
quiz.explain: `into_iter()` on an owned `Vec` takes ownership and yields its elements by value.

concepts.name: Lifetime annotations
concepts.summary: Read and write lifetime parameters like 'a that tell the compiler how returned references relate to inputs.
concepts.why: Lifetimes appear in signatures as soon as a function returns a reference or a struct holds one.
concepts.body:
Every reference has a **lifetime**: the region of code during which it is valid. Usually the compiler infers them. Annotations are needed when a function's signature alone does not say which input a returned reference comes from.

```rust
fn longer<'a>(x: &'a str, y: &'a str) -> &'a str
```

reads as: "for some lifetime `'a`, both inputs live at least as long as `'a`, and the result is valid for `'a`". In practice the result is valid only as long as the shorter of the two inputs. Annotations never change how long anything lives; they describe relationships so the borrow checker can verify callers.

You rarely write them, thanks to the **lifetime elision** rules, which let you leave them out in common situations:

- Each reference parameter gets its own lifetime.
- If there is exactly one input lifetime, it is assigned to all output references.
- In methods with `&self` or `&mut self`, outputs get the lifetime of `self`.

So `fn first_word(s: &str) -> &str` needs nothing, but `longer` above does, because there are two inputs and no `self`.

A struct that holds a reference must declare a lifetime parameter: `struct Parser<'a> { input: &'a str }`. A `Parser` then cannot outlive the string it reads. In `impl<'a> Parser<'a>` you can return `&'a str` slices that stay valid even after the parser itself is dropped.

`'static` means "valid for the whole program": string literals are `&'static str`. Seeing a compiler suggestion to add `'static` is usually a hint that you should return an owned value instead.

When fighting lifetimes in your own structs, ask whether the struct should simply own its data (`String` instead of `&str`). Borrowing structs are great for short-lived views and parsers, not for long-lived state.
takeaways: Lifetime annotations describe relationships between references; they never extend a value's life
Elision covers single-input and `&self` methods; otherwise annotate
Structs holding references need `<'a>` and cannot outlive the borrowed data
pitfalls: Annotating `-> &'static str` to silence an error, when returning an owned `String` is the real fix.

quiz.q: Why does `fn pick(x: &str, y: &str) -> &str` need an explicit lifetime?
options: There are two input references and no self, so elision cannot pick one
Return types can never be references
It does not; it compiles as is
quiz.explain: With multiple input lifetimes and no `self`, the elision rules do not assign an output lifetime.

concepts.name: Testing
concepts.summary: Write unit tests with #[test] and assert macros, whole-library tests in tests/, examples that double as tests, and run them all with cargo test.
concepts.why: Testing is built into Cargo, and well-tested crates are the norm in Rust.
concepts.body:
A test is a function marked `#[test]`: code that runs your code and checks the result. It passes if it returns normally and fails if it panics. The checks are **assertions**, written as macros: `assert!(cond)`, `assert_eq!(left, right)`, `assert_ne!`, each with optional format arguments for a custom message. `assert_eq!` prints both values on failure, so the compared types must implement `Debug` and `PartialEq`.

**Unit tests** check one small piece, such as a single function. By convention they live in the same file as the code, in a child module:

```rust
#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;
    #[test]
    fn works() { assert_eq!(add(2, 2), 4); }
}
```

`#[cfg(test)]` compiles the module only for `cargo test`, and because it is a child module it can test private functions.

**Integration tests** check that the parts work together. They go in the `tests/` folder; each file there is a separate crate that uses your library the way another program would, through its public items only.

**Doc tests**: code examples in `///` documentation comments are compiled and run by `cargo test`, which keeps the examples in your documentation honest.

Other tools:

- A test can return `Result<(), E>` and use `?`; returning `Err` fails it.
- `#[should_panic(expected = "divide by zero")]` asserts a panic with matching message.
- `#[ignore]` skips slow tests unless you run `cargo test -- --ignored`.
- `cargo test parse` runs only tests whose names contain `parse`; `cargo test -- --nocapture` shows `println!` output.

Tests run at the same time on several threads by default, so tests that touch the same file or the same setting can interfere with each other: give each its own file, or run `cargo test -- --test-threads=1`. Popular extra crates are `proptest`, which tries your code on many generated inputs, and `insta`, which compares output with a saved copy.
takeaways: `#[test]` functions pass unless they panic; use `assert_eq!` for good failure output
Unit tests sit in a `#[cfg(test)] mod tests` and can reach private items
`tests/` holds integration tests; `///` examples run as doc tests
pitfalls: Tests that share a temporary file or setting and fail randomly because tests run at the same time.

quiz.q: Where should a test go that should only exercise your crate's public API?
quiz.explain: Each file in `tests/` is compiled as a separate crate, so it can only use public items.

concepts.name: Box, Rc and RefCell
concepts.summary: Put values on the heap with Box, share ownership with Rc, and change shared data with RefCell.
concepts.why: Some data needs more than plain references: a type that contains itself, or a value with several owners, as in trees and graphs.
concepts.body:
A **pointer** is a value that holds the address of another value in the computer's memory; a reference is one kind. A **smart pointer** is a struct that owns data and acts like a pointer by implementing `Deref` (so `*p` and method calls reach the inner value) and `Drop` (cleanup when it goes away). `String` and `Vec` are smart pointers too.

**`Box<T>`** stores a `T` on the heap with a single owner. Use it for:

- **recursive** types, which contain a value of their own type, like a list whose rest is another list: `enum List { Cons(i32, Box<List>), Nil }`. Without the box, the size would be infinite,
- trait objects such as `Box<dyn Error>` and `Box<dyn Fn()>` (a later lesson),
- moving a large value around cheaply by moving only the pointer.

**`Rc<T>`** allows **multiple owners** of the same value, using **reference counting**: it keeps a count of how many owners there are. It is for code that doesn't share data between threads (covered later). `Rc::clone(&rc)` increments a counter instead of copying the data, and the value is dropped when the last `Rc` goes away. `Rc::strong_count` shows the count. Data inside an `Rc` is read-only, because shared ownership implies shared references.

**`RefCell<T>`** moves the borrowing rules from compile time to runtime. `cell.borrow()` returns a guard acting like `&T`, `cell.borrow_mut()` one acting like `&mut T`, and violating "many readers or one writer" **panics** instead of failing to compile. `try_borrow_mut` returns a `Result` instead.

Combined, **`Rc<RefCell<T>>`** gives shared, mutable data: a common shape for graphs and for state shared by several parts of a user interface. Use it sparingly; it is a sign that ownership is genuinely shared, not a way around thinking about ownership.

Two reference-counted values pointing at each other never reach a count of zero, which **leaks** memory. Break cycles with **`Weak<T>`** (`Rc::downgrade`), a non-owning pointer you `upgrade()` to an `Option<Rc<T>>`, typically for parent links in trees.

`Rc` and `RefCell` can't be shared between threads; for that, later lessons use `Arc` and `Mutex`.
takeaways: `Box<T>`: single owner on the heap, for recursive types and trait objects
`Rc<T>`: shared ownership by reference counting, read-only, not for sharing between threads
`RefCell<T>`: borrow rules checked at runtime (panics on violation); break `Rc` cycles with `Weak`
pitfalls: Holding a `borrow()` guard while calling code that does `borrow_mut()` on the same cell, which panics.

quiz.q: What happens if you call `cell.borrow_mut()` while a `cell.borrow()` guard is still alive?
options: It waits until the guard is dropped
The program panics with a BorrowMutError
quiz.explain: `RefCell` enforces the borrow rules at runtime and panics when they are broken.

quiz.q: Two `Rc` nodes point to each other. What happens when all outside handles are dropped?
options: Rust detects the cycle and frees them
The memory leaks because each count stays at 1
quiz.explain: Reference counting cannot collect cycles; one direction should use `Weak` instead.

concepts.name: Lifetimes in depth
concepts.summary: Outlives bounds, what T: 'static really means, higher-ranked bounds, and how impl Trait captures lifetimes in Rust 2024.
concepts.why: Library function signatures, starting threads and async tasks, and functions that take closures all hinge on these less obvious lifetime rules.
concepts.body:
Lifetimes form a hierarchy: `'b: 'a` ("`'b` outlives `'a`") means anything valid for `'b` is valid for `'a`, so a `&'static str` can be used where a `&'a str` is expected. The same syntax applies to types: **`T: 'a`** means every reference inside `T` lives at least as long as `'a`.

**`T: 'static`** is the most misread bound. It does not mean the value lives forever. It means `T` contains no borrowed data shorter than `'static`, so the holder may keep it as long as it likes. `String`, `Vec<u8>` and `Arc<Mutex<X>>` are all `'static` types even though they are dropped normally. `thread::spawn` and `tokio::spawn` require `F: 'static` because the new thread or task may keep running after the function that started it has returned; that is why you `move` owned data in rather than borrowing locals.

**Higher-ranked trait bounds** say "for every lifetime": `F: for<'x> Fn(&'x str) -> &'x str` accepts a closure that works on input of any lifetime, rather than for one particular lifetime chosen by the caller. You mostly see them implicitly, since `Fn(&str) -> &str` is sugar for exactly that.

Reborrowing is why passing a `&mut T` to a function does not move it: the compiler inserts `&mut *r`, a shorter borrow, and you can use `r` again afterwards.

In the **2024 edition**, a return-position `impl Trait` automatically captures every generic parameter and lifetime in scope. When a returned value (an iterator, say) should not be tied to some input, opt out with **precise capturing**: `fn ids(&self) -> impl Iterator<Item = u32> + use<>` (or list exactly which parameters it uses, e.g. `use<'a, T>`).

Finally, trait object lifetimes have defaults: `Box<dyn Trait>` means `Box<dyn Trait + 'static>`, while `&'a dyn Trait` means `&'a (dyn Trait + 'a)`. Write `Box<dyn Trait + 'a>` to store borrowing objects.
takeaways: `T: 'static` means 'owns its data', not 'lives forever'
`for<'x>` bounds accept callbacks that work for any input lifetime
Rust 2024 `impl Trait` returns capture all lifetimes; narrow with `use<..>`
`Box<dyn Trait>` defaults to `+ 'static`
pitfalls: Trying to satisfy `'static` by leaking or making data global, when cloning or `Arc` would do.

quiz.q: Which of these types satisfies `T: 'static`?
quiz.explain: `String` owns its contents and holds no non-static references, so it meets the bound even though it is dropped normally.

quiz.q: In Rust 2024, what does `-> impl Iterator<Item = u8> + use<>` on a `&self` method say?
options: The returned type captures no generic or lifetime parameters
quiz.explain: `use<>` is precise capturing with an empty list, so the hidden type cannot depend on `self`'s lifetime.

concepts.name: Trait objects and dyn
concepts.summary: Use dyn Trait to pick the actual type while the program runs, understand vtables and fat pointers, and know which traits can be used this way.
concepts.why: Add-on systems, lists that mix different types, and errors of any type in a `Box` need the type chosen while the program runs, which generics can't do.
concepts.body:
Generics pick the concrete type at compile time. A **trait object**, `dyn Trait`, picks it at runtime. Because the size of the actual type behind it is unknown, a trait object always sits behind a pointer: `&dyn Draw`, `Box<dyn Draw>`, `Rc<dyn Draw>` or `Arc<dyn Draw + Send + Sync>`.

Such a pointer is a **fat pointer**: two words, one pointing to the data and one to a **vtable**, a static table holding the concrete type's method pointers plus its size, alignment and drop function. Calling a method means looking it up in the vtable first, which is called **dynamic dispatch**. That costs a little (mostly because the compiler can no longer paste the method's code into the caller), but you get one compiled copy of the calling code and can mix types in one collection: `Vec<Box<dyn Draw>>`.

Not every trait can be a trait object. A trait is **dyn compatible** (formerly "object safe") only if its methods could be called through a vtable, which rules out:

- generic methods (`fn visit<T>(&self, t: T)`), since the vtable cannot hold a version for every possible type,
- methods that mention `Self` anywhere except the `self` parameter, such as returning `Self`,
- associated constants, and static functions without `self`.

You can keep such methods on an otherwise compatible trait by adding `where Self: Sized`, which excludes them from the vtable. `Clone` is not dyn compatible, so cloning trait objects in a `Box` needs a helper method like `fn box_clone(&self) -> Box<dyn Shape>`.

Since Rust 1.86, **trait upcasting** works: if `trait Shape: Debug`, a `&dyn Shape` coerces to `&dyn Debug`. To get back the concrete type, use `std::any::Any` and `downcast_ref::<T>()`.

Rule of thumb: generics by default; `dyn` when you need a heterogeneous collection, want shorter compile times or a smaller executable, or need to choose implementations at runtime.
takeaways: `dyn Trait` lives behind a pointer that carries a vtable: one copy of code, indirect calls
Generic methods and `Self`-returning methods break dyn compatibility unless `where Self: Sized`
Use `dyn` for heterogeneous collections and runtime choice; generics otherwise
pitfalls: Defaulting to `Box<dyn Trait>` everywhere out of habit from object-oriented languages like Java, where generics would be simpler and faster.

quiz.q: Why can't `trait Visitor { fn visit<T: Debug>(&self, t: T); }` be used as `dyn Visitor`?
options: Traits with Debug bounds are never dyn compatible
dyn requires all methods to take self by value
A vtable cannot contain an entry for every possible T
quiz.explain: Generic methods would need one vtable entry per instantiation, so they make the trait dyn incompatible.

quiz.q: What is stored in a `&dyn Shape` reference?
options: A pointer to the data and a pointer to a vtable
Only a pointer to the data
A type ID and the value
quiz.explain: Trait object references are fat pointers combining the data pointer with the concrete type's vtable.

concepts.name: Custom errors, thiserror and anyhow
concepts.summary: Design error types with std::error::Error, derive them with thiserror in libraries, and add context with anyhow in applications.
concepts.why: Good error types make failures diagnosable; the thiserror/anyhow split is the ecosystem's standard pattern.
concepts.body:
A proper error type implements **`std::error::Error`**, which requires `Debug` and `Display`, and optionally provides `source()` to expose the underlying cause. Callers can then print it, box it as `Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync>`, and walk the chain of causes.

For a **library**, define an enum of the failures callers might want to react to:

```rust
#[derive(Debug, thiserror::Error)]
pub enum ConfigError {
    #[error("cannot read {path}")]
    Io { path: String, #[source] source: std::io::Error },
    #[error("invalid port {0}")]
    BadPort(u32),
    #[error(transparent)]
    Parse(#[from] std::num::ParseIntError),
}
```

The **thiserror** derive writes the `Display`, `Error::source` and `From` impls you would otherwise write by hand; it adds nothing to your public API. Keep variants meaningful: callers match on them.

For an **application**, you usually just want to report what went wrong with enough context. **anyhow** provides `anyhow::Result<T>` (with an `anyhow::Error` that wraps any error), `.context("loading config")` and `.with_context(|| format!(...))` on both `Result` and `Option`, plus `bail!` and `ensure!` macros. Printing with `{:#}` shows the whole cause chain on one line, and `{:?}` adds a backtrace (the list of function calls that led to the error) when the environment variable `RUST_BACKTRACE=1` is set.

Guidelines that hold up:

- Do not put the source error's message into your own `Display` and also return it from `source()`, or reporters print it twice.
- Make library errors `Send + Sync + 'static` so they work across threads and async tasks.
- Mark public error enums `#[non_exhaustive]` if you may add variants later.
- Libraries should not depend on anyhow in their public API; applications can freely mix both.

The example below implements the same pattern without crates, so you can see what the derive generates.
takeaways: Error types implement `Debug + Display + Error`, exposing causes via `source()`
Libraries: specific enums, often derived with thiserror
Applications: anyhow with `.context()` for readable chains
pitfalls: Returning `Result<T, String>` from libraries, which callers cannot match on or chain.

quiz.q: Which crate split is the common convention?
options: anyhow in libraries, thiserror in applications
thiserror for library error types, anyhow in applications
quiz.explain: Libraries expose precise matchable types (thiserror), while applications mostly report errors with context (anyhow).

concepts.name: Interior mutability: Cell, OnceCell, LazyLock
concepts.summary: Mutate through shared references safely with Cell, RefCell, OnceCell and LazyLock, and see how UnsafeCell underpins them all.
concepts.why: Counters, values computed on first use, program-wide settings and caches all rely on interior mutability, and choosing the right cell avoids panics and locks.
concepts.body:
Normally `&T` means "read-only". **Interior mutability** is the controlled way around that rule: types that allow changes through a shared reference and keep things safe some other way. They all build on **`UnsafeCell<T>`**, the only legal way in Rust to change data reachable through `&`. Every other approach is **undefined behaviour**: breaking a rule the compiler relies on, after which the program may do anything at all.

Single-threaded cells (not `Sync`):

- **`Cell<T>`**: no borrowing at all. You `get` a copy (for `Copy` types), `set`, `replace` or `take` the whole value. No extra cost, and it can never panic. Ideal for counters and flags.
- **`RefCell<T>`**: hands out `Ref`/`RefMut` guards and tracks borrows at runtime, panicking when two borrows clash. Use when you need references into the value.
- **`OnceCell<T>`**: written at most once; `get_or_init(|| ...)` computes on first use. Good for lazily computed fields.
- **`LazyCell<T, F>`**: an `OnceCell` bundled with its initializer.

Thread-safe equivalents:

- **`OnceLock<T>`** (since 1.70) and **`LazyLock<T>`** (since 1.80) for lazily initialised globals: `static CONFIG: LazyLock<Config> = LazyLock::new(load);`. They replace the `lazy_static` and `once_cell` crates.
- **atomics** (`AtomicUsize`, `AtomicBool`) are the thread-safe `Cell` for integers and flags: each change is an **atomic operation**, which can't be seen half-done by another thread.
- **`Mutex<T>`/`RwLock<T>`** are the thread-safe `RefCell`: they block instead of panicking.

Avoid `static mut`: in the 2024 edition, taking a reference to one is denied by default (the `static_mut_refs` lint), because it invites bugs where two threads, or two references, change the same value at once. Use an atomic, a `Mutex`, or a `LazyLock` instead.

Interior mutability is a tool for caches, remembering computed results, reference-counted graphs and statistics kept behind `&self` methods. If you can restructure so that one owner holds `&mut`, that is usually simpler.
takeaways: All interior mutability is built on `UnsafeCell`
`Cell` for small `Copy` values, `RefCell` for borrowed access, `OnceCell` for compute-once
Use `LazyLock`/`OnceLock`, atomics or `Mutex` for globals; avoid `static mut`
pitfalls: Using `RefCell` where `Cell` would do and paying for (and risking) runtime borrow panics.

quiz.q: You need a lazily initialised global configuration readable from many threads. What fits best?
quiz.explain: `LazyLock` is thread-safe, initialises once on first access, and needs no unsafe code.

concepts.name: Threads and scoped threads
concepts.summary: Start threads, move data into them, wait for their results, and borrow local data safely with thread::scope.
concepts.why: Threads let a program do several things at the same moment on a multi-core processor, and Rust's type rules are what make them free of data races.
concepts.body:
A **thread** is one line of work inside a running program. A program can run several threads at the same time, sharing the same memory, like several cooks in one kitchen. Every program starts with one, the **main thread**.

`std::thread::spawn` starts a new operating-system thread running a closure and returns a `JoinHandle<T>`. Calling `join()` waits for it to finish and returns `Result<T, _>`: `Ok` with the closure's return value, or `Err` if the thread panicked. A panic in a spawned thread does not crash the main thread by itself.

The closure must be `Send + 'static`. `'static` because the new thread could outlive the function that spawned it, so it cannot borrow the caller's locals; `Send` because its captured values move to another thread. Hence the usual pattern: a `move` closure that takes ownership of what it needs, cloning or wrapping in `Arc` anything shared.

Since Rust 1.63, **scoped threads** remove the `'static` requirement when threads finish before the function returns:

```rust
std::thread::scope(|s| {
    s.spawn(|| work(&data[..half]));
    s.spawn(|| work(&data[half..]));
}); // all scoped threads are joined here
```

The scope guarantees every thread is joined before it ends, so borrowing local data is safe, and the usual borrow rules still prevent two threads from mutating the same thing.

A **data race** is two threads touching the same data at the same time, with at least one of them changing it; the result depends on luck. In Rust, sharing data between threads without protection is a compile error, not a bug that shows up once a month. That is where the slogan "fearless **concurrency**" (doing several things during the same period) comes from. Data races are impossible in safe Rust, although **deadlocks** (threads waiting for each other forever) and other timing mistakes still are.

- `std::thread::available_parallelism()` tells you how many threads make sense.
- Threads are fairly heavy: each has its own stack, 2 MiB by default for spawned threads. For thousands of tasks that mostly wait, for the network for example, use async (a later lesson). For heavy calculations spread over all processor cores (**parallelism**), the **rayon** crate turns `iter()` into `par_iter()` and shares the work among a fixed set of threads.
- `thread::Builder` sets names and stack sizes; `thread::sleep` pauses the current thread.
takeaways: `thread::spawn` needs a `Send + 'static` closure, so `move` owned data in
`join()` returns the result, or `Err` if the thread panicked
`thread::scope` lets threads borrow local data because they are joined before it returns
pitfalls: Spawning a thread per small task; use a pool (rayon) or async for many tiny units of work.

quiz.q: Why can a closure passed to `thread::scope`'s `s.spawn` borrow a local Vec, but one passed to `thread::spawn` cannot?
options: The scope joins all its threads before returning, so borrows cannot outlive the data
thread::spawn runs on the same thread
Scoped threads are not real OS threads
quiz.explain: Because the scope guarantees completion before it ends, the borrow checker can verify the borrows; plain `spawn` requires `'static`.

concepts.name: Arc, Mutex and RwLock
concepts.summary: Share data across threads with Arc, protect changes with Mutex or RwLock, use atomics for counters, and avoid deadlocks.
concepts.why: Any program whose threads work on common data needs these standard building blocks.
concepts.body:
To share ownership across threads you need **`Arc<T>`**, the thread-safe version of `Rc` (the name means atomically reference counted). Cloning an `Arc` increases its count with an atomic operation, so two threads can't garble it; the data is read-only through it.

To change shared data, protect it with a **lock**, something only one thread can hold at a time. Rust's basic lock is the **mutex** (short for mutual exclusion): **`Arc<Mutex<T>>`**. `mutex.lock()` waits until it gets exclusive access and returns a `MutexGuard`, which derefs to `&mut T` and **unlocks when dropped**. There is no separate `unlock` call to forget; keep critical sections short by limiting the guard's scope with a block or an explicit `drop(guard)`.

`lock()` returns a `Result` because of **poisoning**: if a thread panics while holding the guard, the mutex is marked poisoned, since the data might be half-updated. Most code calls `.unwrap()` (propagating the panic) or recovers with `.unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner())`.

**`RwLock<T>`** allows many readers (`read()`) or one writer (`write()`); it helps when reads dominate and are long. For short critical sections a `Mutex` is often faster.

For simple counters and flags, **atomics** like `AtomicU64` avoid locks entirely: `counter.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed)`. Memory orderings beyond `Relaxed` (`Acquire`/`Release`, `SeqCst`) matter when the atomic guards other data; if unsure, use `SeqCst` or a `Mutex`.

Deadlocks are still possible: two threads taking locks A then B and B then A. Always take several locks in the same fixed order, and never call code you don't control (such as a closure passed in to you) while holding a lock. A thread that tries to lock a `Mutex` it already holds waits for itself forever: std mutexes can't be locked twice by the same thread.

Alternatives: `parking_lot` offers smaller, faster locks without poisoning; channels avoid shared state altogether.
takeaways: `Arc` shares ownership across threads; `Mutex`/`RwLock` add mutation
Guards unlock on drop; keep them in the smallest possible scope
Use atomics for counters and a fixed lock order to avoid deadlocks
pitfalls: Locking a `Mutex` twice on the same thread (for example in a helper called while holding the guard), which deadlocks.

quiz.q: What happens to a std `Mutex` if a thread panics while holding its guard?
options: The data is reset to default
Nothing; the guard is just dropped
The mutex becomes poisoned and later lock() calls return Err
quiz.explain: Poisoning signals the data may be inconsistent; `lock()` then returns `Err(PoisonError)`, from which you can still recover the guard.

quiz.q: Why is `Rc<RefCell<T>>` rejected by `thread::spawn` while `Arc<Mutex<T>>` is accepted?
options: Rc's counter and RefCell's borrow flag are not thread-safe, so they are not Send/Sync
quiz.explain: Non-atomic reference counts and borrow flags would race, so those types do not implement `Send`/`Sync`.

concepts.name: Message passing with channels
concepts.summary: Pass values between threads through channels, use bounded channels so fast senders slow down, and shut down cleanly.
concepts.why: Channels let threads cooperate by passing ownership instead of sharing memory, which is often simpler and safer.
concepts.body:
A **channel** is like a conveyor belt between threads: producer threads put values on one end and a consumer thread takes them off the other. `std::sync::mpsc::channel()` returns a `(Sender<T>, Receiver<T>)` pair; mpsc stands for multiple producer, single consumer. Clone the `Sender` to give one to each producer thread.

Sending **moves** the value into the channel, so the sender cannot touch it afterwards: ownership transfers to the receiving thread and no locking of the data is needed.

Receiving:

- `rx.recv()` waits until a message arrives, returning `Err` once **all senders are dropped** and the channel is empty.
- `for msg in rx` (or `rx.iter()`) loops until that happens, which gives you clean shutdown for free: when producers finish and drop their senders, the consumer's loop ends.
- `try_recv()` never waits; `recv_timeout(d)` waits up to a duration.

The classic mistake: keeping the original `tx` alive in the main thread after cloning it for the worker threads. The consumer then waits forever, because one sender still exists. `drop(tx)` once you have handed out the clones.

`channel()` is unbounded: a fast producer can fill memory. **`sync_channel(n)`** is bounded; `send` waits when `n` messages are queued, which slows a fast producer down to the consumer's pace. This is called **backpressure**. `sync_channel(0)` is a rendezvous channel where each send waits for a matching receive.

To send different kinds of messages, send an enum. To get a reply, include a `Sender` for the answer inside the message. A thread that owns some data and only talks through messages like this is called an actor.

For multiple consumers or `select` over several channels, use the `crossbeam-channel` crate; for async code (a later lesson), use the channels in `tokio::sync` (`mpsc`, `oneshot`, `broadcast`, `watch`).
takeaways: Sending moves ownership to the receiving thread; no locks on the data
The receiving loop ends when all `Sender`s are dropped
Use `sync_channel(n)` for backpressure; enums for several message kinds
pitfalls: Forgetting to drop the original `Sender`, so the receiving loop hangs forever.

quiz.q: Workers each got a clone of `tx`, and they all finished. Why might `for m in rx` still hang?
options: Channels must be closed with rx.close()
The original tx in the spawning thread is still alive
quiz.explain: The receiver only sees the channel close when every sender, including the original, has been dropped.

concepts.name: async/await and futures
concepts.summary: Understand what async fn returns, why futures are lazy, how executors poll them, and when async beats threads.
concepts.why: Network services in Rust are overwhelmingly async, and its poll-based model explains many of its rules and errors.
concepts.body:
Some programs spend most of their time waiting, for a network reply or a timer, say. **Asynchronous** (async) code lets one thread juggle many such tasks: while one waits, another runs.

An `async fn` does not run when called. It returns a **future**, a value standing for work that will finish later: a value implementing `std::future::Future`, a **state machine** the compiler generates from your function, which remembers which `.await` it has reached. Nothing happens until something **polls** it, that is, asks it to make progress. **`.await`** inside another async context drives a future to completion, suspending the current task whenever the inner future is not ready.

The trait is small:

```rust
trait Future {
    type Output;
    fn poll(self: Pin<&mut Self>, cx: &mut Context<'_>) -> Poll<Self::Output>;
}
```

`poll` returns `Poll::Ready(value)` or `Poll::Pending`. When pending, the future stores the **`Waker`** from `cx`; when the data or timer it waits for is ready, it calls `wake()`, telling the **executor** (the code that runs futures) to poll it again. No thread is blocked while waiting.

The standard library defines the trait but ships **no executor**. You choose an async runtime (Tokio, smol, or embassy for small devices) that polls tasks, plus a part that asks the operating system to report when network data or files are ready. The example builds a tiny executor using only std to show the mechanics.

Key consequences:

- Async is **cooperative**: a task gives up the thread only at `.await`. A long calculation, or a **blocking** call that makes the thread sit and wait (like `std::thread::sleep` or ordinary file reading), stalls every task sharing that thread.
- Async pays off when many things wait at once, such as thousands of network connections, with little calculation each. For heavy calculation spread over processor cores, threads or rayon are simpler.
- Futures can be **cancelled** by simply dropping them, which means code after an `.await` might never run.

Other syntax: `async { ... }` blocks create futures right where they are written, `async move` takes ownership of what it captures, **async closures** `async |x| ...` are stable since 1.85, and `async fn` is allowed in traits since 1.75.
takeaways: `async fn` returns a lazy future; `.await` drives it
Executors poll futures; wakers tell them when to poll again
Never block inside async code: tasks only yield at `.await`
pitfalls: Calling an async function without `.await` and wondering why nothing happened (the compiler warns: futures do nothing unless awaited).

quiz.q: What happens when you call `fetch()` (an async fn) without `.await` and drop the result?
options: Nothing: the future is never polled
quiz.explain: Futures are inert until polled, so dropping one un-awaited means its body never executes.

quiz.q: Why does `std::thread::sleep` inside an async task harm other tasks?
options: It blocks the worker thread, so no other task on it can be polled
quiz.explain: Async scheduling is cooperative; a blocking call holds the thread and starves every task sharing it.

concepts.name: Tokio basics
concepts.summary: Run async code on the Tokio runtime: #[tokio::main], spawn, join!, select!, timeouts, async channels and spawn_blocking.
concepts.why: Tokio is the de facto async runtime behind axum, reqwest, tonic and most Rust network services.
concepts.body:
**Tokio** provides the executor, timers, network and file access that work with async, and async versions of locks and channels. Add it with `cargo add tokio --features full` (or pick features like `rt-multi-thread`, `macros`, `net`, `time`, `sync`).

`#[tokio::main]` turns `async fn main` into a normal `main` that starts Tokio's runtime, which by default runs tasks on several threads and lets idle threads take over waiting work, and then runs your future to completion. `#[tokio::test]` does the same for tests.

Concurrency tools:

- **`tokio::spawn(fut)`** runs a future as an independent task, possibly on another worker thread, and returns a `JoinHandle` you can `.await` for the result (an `Err` if it panicked). Spawned futures must be `Send + 'static`, so `move` owned or `Arc`'d data in.
- **`tokio::join!(a, b)`** runs futures concurrently within the current task and waits for all; `try_join!` stops at the first error.
- **`tokio::select!`** waits on several futures and runs the branch of whichever finishes first, **dropping (cancelling) the others**. It is the building block for time limits, shutdown signals and "whichever server answers first".
- **`tokio::time::timeout(dur, fut)`** and `sleep` for timing; never `std::thread::sleep`.

For shared state, `std::sync::Mutex` is fine if you never hold the guard across an `.await` (the compiler usually stops you anyway, because the guard is not `Send`). If you must hold a lock across `.await`, use `tokio::sync::Mutex`. Async channels live in `tokio::sync`: `mpsc`, `oneshot` for a single reply, `broadcast`, and `watch` for latest-value state.

Blocking or CPU-heavy work goes to **`tokio::task::spawn_blocking`**, which runs it on a separate **thread pool** (a set of threads kept ready for such work) and gives you a future for the result.

A useful mental model: `join!` and `select!` give concurrency inside one task; `spawn` gives you new tasks that can run in parallel.
takeaways: `#[tokio::main]` starts the runtime; `tokio::spawn` creates `Send + 'static` tasks
`join!` waits for all, `select!` takes the first and cancels the rest
Use `tokio::time` and `spawn_blocking`; never block a worker thread
pitfalls: Holding a `std::sync::MutexGuard` across `.await`; scope the guard or use `tokio::sync::Mutex`.

quiz.q: In `tokio::select! { a = fut_a => ..., b = fut_b => ... }`, what happens to fut_b if fut_a finishes first?
options: It keeps running in the background
quiz.explain: `select!` runs the first ready branch and drops the remaining futures, cancelling them.

concepts.name: Declarative macros (macro_rules!)
concepts.summary: Write macro_rules! macros with fragment specifiers and repetitions, understand hygiene, and export them from a crate.
concepts.why: Macros remove repetitive code that functions can't, such as taking any number of arguments or writing the same impl for many types.
concepts.body:
A **declarative macro** matches the code you pass it against patterns and expands into new code, at compile time. `vec!`, `println!` and `matches!` are examples. Use one when a function cannot do the job: a variable number of arguments, generating items (functions, impls) for many types, or taking code fragments as input.

```rust
macro_rules! square {
    ($x:expr) => { $x * $x };
}
```

Each rule is `(matcher) => { transcriber }`, tried top to bottom. Metavariables carry a **fragment specifier**: `expr`, `ident`, `ty`, `pat`, `path`, `block`, `stmt`, `literal`, `lifetime`, `vis`, `item`, `meta`, and `tt` (a **token tree**: one word, number or punctuation mark of code, or a whole bracketed group; the most flexible).

**Repetitions** `$( ... ),*` match zero or more comma-separated items (`+` for one or more, `?` for optional) and are expanded with the same `$( ... )*` syntax in the output. A rule can call the macro again on the rest of its input (recursion), to handle the input piece by piece.

Macros are partly **hygienic**: local variables created inside the expansion cannot clash with the caller's variables. Item names (functions, types) are not hygienic, and paths are resolved at the call site, so macros meant for other crates should refer to their own crate as `$crate::path::item`.

Two classic gotchas: an `expr` argument is substituted as one unit, so `square!(1 + 2)` gives 9, but it is also **evaluated as many times** as it appears; bind it with `let v = $x;` to evaluate once. And macros must be defined before use in textual order inside a crate.

To make a macro usable from other crates, add `#[macro_export]`; it then lives at the crate root and can be imported with `use my_crate::my_macro;`. Debug expansions with `cargo expand` (a separate tool).
takeaways: Rules match code patterns with fragment specifiers like `expr`, `ident`, `ty`, `tt`
`$( ... ),*` repeats in both matcher and expansion
Bind `expr` arguments once; use `$crate::` and `#[macro_export]` for macros used by other crates
pitfalls: Writing a macro where a generic function would work; macros are harder to read, debug and document.

quiz.q: Given `macro_rules! double { ($x:expr) => { $x + $x }; }`, how many times does `double!(next())` call next()?
quiz.explain: The expression is pasted into each place it appears, so it is evaluated twice; bind it to a local first.

concepts.name: Unsafe Rust and raw pointers
concepts.summary: What unsafe allows, raw pointers and &raw, writing sound safe abstractions, SAFETY comments, the 2024 edition rules and Miri.
concepts.why: The standard library, FFI and high-performance data structures rest on unsafe code; using it soundly is an expert skill.
concepts.body:
`unsafe` does not turn off the borrow checker. It allows five extra operations whose safety the compiler cannot verify:

- dereferencing a **raw pointer** (`*const T`, `*mut T`),
- calling an `unsafe fn` (including foreign functions),
- reading or writing a `static mut`,
- implementing an `unsafe trait` such as `Send` or `Sync`,
- reading fields of a `union`.

An `unsafe` block is your promise that you have kept the rules the compiler normally checks. If you are wrong, the result is **undefined behaviour (UB)**: not just a crash, but permission for the compiler's optimisations to assume impossible things and miscompile surrounding safe code. Examples of UB: creating a dangling or misaligned reference, two live `&mut` to the same data, reading uninitialised memory, a `bool` that is not 0 or 1, data races.

A **raw pointer** may be null, may point at freed memory, or may overlap with other pointers; creating them is safe, only dereferencing is unsafe. Use `&raw const x` / `&raw mut x` (stable since 1.82) to get a pointer without first creating a reference, which matters for unaligned or uninitialised fields.

The goal is a **safe abstraction**: a small unsafe core behind a safe API whose every possible use is sound, like `Vec` or `split_at_mut`. **Soundness** (no possible use of the safe API can cause UB) is a property of the whole module, since safe code in the same module can break rules that the unsafe code relies on. Document each block with a `// SAFETY:` comment saying why the requirements hold, and each `unsafe fn` with a `# Safety` doc section listing caller obligations.

The **2024 edition** tightens the rules: operations inside an `unsafe fn` need their own `unsafe {}` block (the `unsafe_op_in_unsafe_fn` lint warns by default), `extern` blocks must be written `unsafe extern`, and attributes such as `no_mangle` become `#[unsafe(no_mangle)]`.

Test unsafe code under **Miri** (`cargo +nightly miri test`), a tool that runs your program step by step and detects many kinds of UB.
takeaways: `unsafe` enables five operations; it does not disable borrow checking
Wrap unsafe code in safe APIs that are sound for every possible caller
Write `// SAFETY:` comments and test with Miri
2024 edition: unsafe blocks inside unsafe fn, `unsafe extern`, `#[unsafe(no_mangle)]`
pitfalls: Assuming code that seems to work is fine; UB can appear only under optimisation or on another compiler version.

quiz.q: Which of these requires an unsafe block?
options: Creating a raw pointer with `&raw const x`
quiz.explain: Creating and comparing raw pointers is safe; only dereferencing them (and the other four superpowers) needs `unsafe`.

quiz.q: A safe function wraps an unsafe block but can cause UB with some valid inputs. What is it called?
quiz.explain: A safe API must be sound for every input; if any safe call can trigger UB, the abstraction is unsound.

concepts.name: Memory layout, repr and niches
concepts.summary: How Rust lays out structs and enums: size and alignment, field reordering, repr(C), repr(transparent), niche optimisation and DSTs.
concepts.why: Layout knowledge matters for calling C code, for unsafe code, for data that uses the processor's cache well, and for understanding why Option<&T> costs nothing.
concepts.body:
Every type has a **size** and an **alignment**: the address of every value must be a multiple of its alignment. The size is always a multiple of the alignment, so that arrays work. Unused bytes added to keep fields aligned are called **padding**. `std::mem::size_of::<T>()` and `align_of::<T>()` report them.

With the default representation, **`repr(Rust)`**, the compiler may **reorder fields** to minimise padding, and the layout is unspecified: it can change between compiler versions. Never assume field order or offsets for a plain struct.

Other representations give guarantees:

- **`#[repr(C)]`**: fields in declaration order with C's padding rules. Required when exchanging values with C (FFI) and for any layout you rely on from unsafe code.
- **`#[repr(transparent)]`**: a struct with one non-zero-sized field has exactly that field's layout and calling convention (**ABI**). Ideal for newtypes passed across FFI.
- **`#[repr(u8)]`** (or another integer) on an enum fixes the discriminant type and values.
- **`#[repr(packed)]`** removes padding, but fields may be misaligned, so taking references to them is an error; read them by copy or through `&raw const`.
- **`#[repr(align(64))]`** raises alignment, e.g. to keep hot atomics on separate cache lines.

**Niche optimisation**: an enum stores which variant it holds in a hidden number, the **discriminant**. When a type has bit patterns that are never valid, enums can use them to store the discriminant for free. References and `Box` are never null, so `Option<&T>` and `Option<Box<T>>` are the size of a pointer, with `None` represented as null. `NonZeroU32` gives the same benefit for integers, and `bool` and `char` have niches too.

**Zero-sized types** (`()`, unit structs, `PhantomData`) take no space, and a `Vec<()>` never allocates. **Dynamically sized types** (`str`, `[T]`, `dyn Trait`) can only be used behind pointers, which become fat: pointer plus length or pointer plus vtable.

Enums are as large as their largest variant plus a discriminant (unless a niche absorbs it). Putting a rarely used large variant in a `Box` keeps the whole enum small; clippy's `large_enum_variant` lint flags this.
takeaways: Default layout is unspecified and may reorder fields; use `repr(C)` when layout matters
Niche optimisation makes `Option<&T>`, `Option<Box<T>>`, `Option<NonZeroU32>` free
DST pointers are fat; ZSTs take no space; box large rare enum variants
pitfalls: Transmuting or casting between `repr(Rust)` structs that look identical; their layouts are not guaranteed to match.

quiz.q: Why is `size_of::<Option<&u64>>()` equal to `size_of::<&u64>()`?
options: The compiler drops the Option at runtime
References are never null, so None is stored as the null pointer
quiz.explain: The null bit pattern is a niche in `&T`, so the enum uses it for `None` and needs no extra tag.

quiz.q: You pass a struct to a C library by pointer. Which attribute do you need?
options: None; Rust matches C by default
quiz.explain: Only `repr(C)` guarantees C-compatible field order and padding.

concepts.name: Send and Sync
concepts.summary: The two auto traits that make data races impossible: what they mean, which std types lack them, and when to implement them unsafely.
concepts.why: Every function that starts a thread or async task is defined in terms of these traits; understanding them explains a whole family of compiler errors.
concepts.body:
Thread safety in Rust is two marker traits with no methods:

- **`Send`**: a value of this type can be **moved** to another thread.
- **`Sync`**: a value can be **shared** between threads by reference. Formally, `T: Sync` exactly when `&T: Send`.

They are **auto traits**: the compiler implements them for your type automatically when all of its fields are `Send`/`Sync`. That is why you rarely think about them until a type that lacks them sneaks into a struct.

Instructive examples in std:

- `Rc<T>` is neither: two threads cloning it would race on the non-atomic count. `Arc<T>` is `Send + Sync` when `T: Send + Sync`.
- `Cell<T>` and `RefCell<T>` are `Send` (if `T: Send`) but not `Sync`: one thread may own and mutate them, but shared access from two threads would race.
- `Mutex<T>` is `Sync` when `T: Send`. That is the whole trick: the lock turns a `Send` type into one that can be shared.
- `MutexGuard` is not `Send`, because some platforms require unlocking on the locking thread. In async code this is why a std guard held across `.await` makes the future non-`Send` and `tokio::spawn` rejects it.
- Raw pointers are neither, as a conservative default so that types built on them must opt in deliberately.

When you build a type on raw pointers that is in fact thread-safe, you implement the traits yourself: `unsafe impl Send for MyBuf {}`. The `unsafe` is the point: you are promising the compiler that every API on the type upholds thread safety, and getting it wrong means data races.

To opt **out** on stable Rust, add a field such as `PhantomData<*const ()>` (neither) or `PhantomData<Cell<()>>` (Send but not Sync). Compile-time checks like `fn assert_send<T: Send>() {}` are a cheap way to make the compiler check the guarantees your API promises.
takeaways: `Send` = can move to another thread; `Sync` = `&T` can be shared across threads
Both are auto traits, derived from the fields
`Rc` is neither, `Cell`/`RefCell` are Send not Sync, `Mutex` makes Send data Sync
Implementing them is `unsafe`; opt out with a `PhantomData` field
pitfalls: Writing `unsafe impl Sync` just to silence a compiler error without proving thread safety.

quiz.q: Which statement is true?
options: RefCell<T> is Sync but not Send
Mutex<T> is Sync whenever T is Send
Rc<T> is Send if T is Send
Raw pointers are Send and Sync
quiz.explain: A `Mutex` serialises access, so it only needs `T: Send` to be shareable (`Sync`).

quiz.q: Why does `tokio::spawn` reject a future holding a `std::sync::MutexGuard` across `.await`?
options: MutexGuard is not Send, so the whole future is not Send
quiz.explain: A future is `Send` only if everything it holds across await points is `Send`, and `MutexGuard` is not.

concepts.name: Variance and PhantomData
concepts.summary: How lifetimes subtype, why &mut T is invariant, and how PhantomData declares ownership, variance and auto traits for unused type parameters.
concepts.why: Writing generic collection types, typed IDs or unsafe code over raw pointers requires getting variance and PhantomData right.
concepts.body:
A **subtype** can be used wherever its parent type is expected. Rust's only subtyping is between lifetimes: `&'static str` is a subtype of `&'a str`, because a longer-lived reference can be used where a shorter one is expected. **Variance** says how that relationship passes through a type constructor:

- **Covariant**: `F<Sub>` is a subtype of `F<Super>`. `&'a T` is covariant in `'a` and `T`; so are `Box<T>`, `Vec<T>` and `*const T`.
- **Invariant**: no subtyping at all. `&'a mut T` is invariant in `T`, as are `Cell<T>`, `UnsafeCell<T>` and `*mut T`.
- **Contravariant**: reversed. `fn(T)` is contravariant in `T`: a function accepting any `&'a str` can stand in for one that only needs `&'static str`.

Why must `&mut T` be invariant? If `&mut &'static str` could shrink to `&mut &'a str`, you could write a short-lived `&'a str` through it and the original owner would later read a dangling `'static` reference. Invariance blocks exactly that.

The compiler infers variance from fields. If a type parameter is not used in any field (common with raw pointers or typed IDs), you must add **`PhantomData<...>`**, a zero-sized marker that tells the compiler how to treat it. Choose the form that describes what you mean:

- `PhantomData<T>`: "I own a `T`" (covariant, affects drop checking and auto traits like a real `T`).
- `PhantomData<&'a T>`: "I borrow a `T` for `'a`", typical for iterators over raw pointers.
- `PhantomData<fn() -> T>`: covariant but does not own a `T`, so the type stays `Send`/`Sync` whatever `T` is. Good for typed IDs.
- `PhantomData<fn(T) -> T>` or `PhantomData<*mut T>`: invariant.

Getting this wrong in unsafe code is a soundness bug: a raw-pointer iterator without `PhantomData<&'a T>` would let callers keep items after the collection is freed.
takeaways: Covariant: `&'a T`, `Box<T>`; invariant: `&mut T`, `Cell<T>`; contravariant: `fn(T)`
`&mut T` is invariant so you cannot smuggle a short-lived value into a long-lived slot
Unused type or lifetime parameters need `PhantomData`; pick the form that states ownership and variance
pitfalls: Using `PhantomData<T>` for a typed ID, which makes `Id<T>` non-Send whenever `T` is; use `PhantomData<fn() -> T>`.

quiz.q: Which type is invariant in T?
quiz.explain: `Cell<T>` allows mutation through a shared reference, so like `&mut T` it must be invariant.

quiz.q: Why does a raw-pointer slice iterator include `PhantomData<&'a T>`?
options: To tie returned references to the slice's lifetime and get correct variance
Because raw pointers need a lifetime to compile
quiz.explain: Raw pointers carry no lifetime, so the marker tells the borrow checker the iterator borrows the slice for `'a`.

concepts.name: Pin and self-referential futures
concepts.summary: Why async state machines can't move, what Pin and Unpin guarantee, how to pin with Box::pin and pin!, and how pin projection works.
concepts.why: Pin shows up whenever you implement Future, store futures or write async combinators, and its rules confuse almost everyone at first.
concepts.body:
An `async` block that keeps a reference to one of its own locals across an `.await` compiles into a **self-referential** struct: one field points into another field of the same struct. If that struct were moved to a new address after the first poll, the internal pointer would point at the old, freed spot. **`Pin

`** wraps a pointer `P` (such as `&mut T` or `Box`) and guarantees that the pointee will **not move again** until it is dropped. That is why `Future::poll` takes `self: Pin<&mut Self>`: once polled, a future stays put. Most types do not care about being moved, so they implement the auto trait **`Unpin`**, and for them `Pin` is a no-op: `Pin::new(&mut x)` works and `get_mut` gives back `&mut T`. Compiler-generated futures are `!Unpin`, as is any type with a `PhantomPinned` field. For those, getting a `&mut T` out of a `Pin` is `unsafe`, because you could `mem::swap` it away. Ways to pin a `!Unpin` value: - **`Box::pin(value)`** pins on the heap; the result `Pin>` is itself `Unpin` and easy to store, e.g. `Pin + Send>>`. - **`std::pin::pin!(value)`** pins on the stack for local use, giving `Pin<&mut T>`. When you write your own future that contains another future, you need **pin projection**: turning `Pin<&mut Outer>` into `Pin<&mut Inner>` for the structurally pinned field and a plain `&mut` for the rest. Doing it by hand requires unsafe code and careful rules (no moving pinned fields, a compatible `Drop`), so use the `pin-project` or `pin-project-lite` crates. Or sidestep it, as in the example, by storing the inner future as `Pin>`, which keeps the outer type `Unpin` at the cost of one extra heap allocation. `Pin` only constrains the pointee's address. It does not make a type immutable, and it is not needed for ordinary code: you meet it when implementing `Future` or `Stream` by hand.
takeaways: Futures may be self-referential, so once polled they must not move

`Pin

` guarantees the pointee stays put; for `Unpin` types it changes nothing
Pin with `Box::pin` or `pin!`; use pin-project (or an inner future in a `Box`) for projection
pitfalls: Thinking `Pin` makes a value immutable; it only forbids moving `!Unpin` values out from behind the pointer.

quiz.q: Why does `Future::poll` take `self: Pin<&mut Self>` instead of `&mut self`?
options: To allow polling from several threads at once
So async state machines that borrow their own fields cannot be moved between polls
quiz.explain: Generated futures can hold internal references; pinning guarantees their address stays stable after the first poll.

quiz.q: For a type that implements `Unpin`, what does `Pin<&mut T>` restrict?
options: Nothing significant: you can get &mut T back with get_mut
quiz.explain: `Unpin` types opt out of pinning guarantees, so `Pin::new` and `get_mut` are both safe.

concepts.name: Procedural macros
concepts.summary: Write procedural macros (derive macros, attribute macros and function-like macros) with syn and quote, and point errors at the user's code.
concepts.why: Serde, Tokio's #[tokio::main], clap and thiserror are all proc macros; writing one removes whole kinds of repetitive code.
concepts.body:
A **procedural macro** is a Rust function that runs inside the compiler: it receives code as a `TokenStream` (a sequence of token trees) and returns new code as another `TokenStream`. There are three kinds:

- **Derive** macros, `#[derive(MyTrait)]`, receive the item and **add** new items (usually an `impl`) without changing the original.
- **Attribute macros**, `#[route(GET, "/")]`, receive the attribute arguments and the item, and **replace** the item with their output.
- **Function-like** macros, `sql!(...)`, receive any code at all, like `macro_rules!` but with full Rust logic.

They must live in their own crate with `[lib] proc-macro = true` in `Cargo.toml`; that crate can only export macros. A common layout is `mylib` (runtime types and traits) plus `mylib-derive` (the macros), with `mylib` re-exporting the derive.

Nobody handles the raw pieces by hand. **`syn`** parses them into a tree of Rust items you can inspect (`DeriveInput`, `ItemFn`, ...), and **`quote`**'s `quote!` macro turns Rust-like templates back into code, with `#var` interpolation and `#(#items),*` repetition.

Quality details that separate a good macro from a painful one:

- **Errors with spans** (a span is the location of a piece of code): return `syn::Error::new_spanned(node, "message").to_compile_error()` instead of panicking, so the error underlines the user's code.
- **Generics**: use `generics.split_for_impl()` so derived impls work on generic types.
- **Full paths**: emit `::std::fmt::Display` or `::mylib::Trait`, since the user may have shadowed names.
- Macros are **unhygienic** by default (`Span::call_site()`); create helper names carefully.

Costs: proc macros add compile time (syn is a large dependency) and can make errors harder to read. Prefer a generic function or `macro_rules!` when they suffice. Test macros with `trybuild` for expected compile errors and inspect output with `cargo expand`.
takeaways: Derive macros add items, attribute macros replace the item, function-like macros take any code
Proc macros live in a `proc-macro = true` crate and usually use syn + quote
Report errors with spans, handle generics, and emit absolute paths
pitfalls: Panicking inside the macro on bad input, which gives users an unhelpful error with no location.

quiz.q: How does a derive macro's output relate to the struct it is applied to?
options: It is appended after the struct, which stays unchanged
quiz.explain: Derive macros can only add new items; attribute macros are the kind that can rewrite the item.

concepts.name: FFI: calling C and being called from C
concepts.summary: Declare foreign functions in unsafe extern blocks, export extern "C" functions, pass strings, structs and callbacks, and keep ownership straight.
concepts.why: Using libraries written in C, running Rust inside C, C++ or Python programs, or gradually rewriting C code all go through FFI.
concepts.body:
Calling code written in another language is called a **foreign function interface (FFI)**. Rust talks to other languages through the **C ABI**: C's rules for how functions pass values and results. To call C, declare the functions in an extern block. In the **2024 edition** the block itself must be marked `unsafe`, and each item can be declared `safe` or `unsafe`:

```rust
unsafe extern "C" {
    pub safe fn abs(x: i32) -> i32;            // callable without unsafe
    pub unsafe fn strlen(s: *const c_char) -> usize;
}
```

Declaring a signature is a promise the compiler cannot check; a wrong type here is undefined behaviour. For real libraries, generate the declarations with **bindgen**, link with `#[link(name = "foo")]` or a `build.rs`, and compile bundled C with the `cc` crate.

To be called from C, export a function: `#[unsafe(no_mangle)] pub extern "C" fn add(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32`, and build a `cdylib` or `staticlib` crate type. **cbindgen** generates the C header.

Types across the boundary must have a C layout: integers, floats, raw pointers, `#[repr(C)]` structs and enums, and `Option<extern "C" fn(...)>` for callbacks that may be missing (a niche makes `None` the null pointer). Use `std::ffi::{c_int, c_char, c_void}` for C types.

Strings: a C string is a run of bytes ended by a zero byte (NUL). **`CString`** owns one you can pass as `.as_ptr()` (keep the `CString` alive while C uses the pointer); **`CStr`** borrows one received from C, and `c"literal"` makes a `&CStr` at compile time.

Ownership rule: memory must be freed by the allocator that created it. Hand Rust objects to C with `Box::into_raw` and provide a `free_thing(ptr)` function that calls `Box::from_raw`.

Panics must not unwind into C. Since Rust 1.81, a panic that reaches the edge of an `extern "C"` function ends the whole program at once; catch panics with `std::panic::catch_unwind` at the boundary, or use the `"C-unwind"` ABI when unwinding across languages is intended.
takeaways: 2024 edition: `unsafe extern "C" { safe fn ...; unsafe fn ...; }` and `#[unsafe(no_mangle)]`
Only C-layout types cross the boundary; use `CString`/`CStr` for strings
Free memory with the allocator that allocated it; never let panics unwind into C
pitfalls: Passing `CString::new(s).unwrap().as_ptr()` directly: the temporary is dropped and the pointer dangles.

quiz.q: What happens if a Rust panic reaches the edge of an `extern "C"` function (Rust 1.81+)?
options: It unwinds into the C caller
quiz.explain: Unwinding through the plain C ABI is not allowed, so the runtime aborts; use catch_unwind or the "C-unwind" ABI.

quiz.q: Rust hands a `Box<Parser>` to C with `Box::into_raw`. How should it be freed?
options: It is freed automatically when the Box goes out of scope
C calls an exported Rust function that uses Box::from_raw
quiz.explain: Memory must be released by the allocator that created it, so Rust exports a destructor that rebuilds and drops the Box.
